news.title: Oversight chair James Comer enters Kentucky governor's race
news.text:
James Comer, the Kentucky Republican who chairs the House Oversight Committee, announced Monday night that he is running for governor in 2027, seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear.

Comer made his announcement during a tele-town hall. He is the first high-profile Republican to enter the race, NBC News reported. Beshear has governed Kentucky since 2019.

For most of the event, Comer took callers’ questions about education, small business and high prices. He said eliminating Kentucky’s income tax would be his top priority as governor.

“Kentucky needs a leader whose policies will lead to growth and good-paying jobs. We need a leader whose priority will be to reduce taxes so Kentuckians can keep more of what they earn,” Comer said.

Kentucky Democratic Party Chair Colmon Elridge criticized Comer’s Washington record in a statement, saying he advanced President Donald Trump’s agenda by “supporting the largest cuts to Medicaid and SNAP in American history while doing nothing to protect Kentuckians from Trump’s costly tariffs and chaotic war in Iran.”

“Very few candidates would have the confidence to run for governor on a record like that, but Jamie Comer has never been one to let facts get in the way of a good story,” Elridge said.

Comer addressed Trump’s national policies when a caller asked a question. “I think that some of the things the president has tried to do on the national level had good intentions, but there are always unintended consequences,” he said.

“Serving this state is a calling for me,” Comer said. He added, “The government doesn’t have all the answers, but we have a responsibility to solve problems and lift people up when we can.”

His campaign launch followed this month’s midterm elections, when Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress, NBC News reported. Trump carried Kentucky by roughly 30 points over Kamala Harris in 2024, according to Fox News.

U.S. Sen. Rand Paul endorsed Comer on X minutes after the announcement video went live.

I’m proud to endorse my friend @JamesComer to be Kentucky’s next Governor! Please help him to get there!— Rand Paul (@RandPaul) November 17, 2026

Agriculture Commissioner Jonathan Shell called into the livestream to endorse Comer. Secretary of State Michael Adams, Attorney General Russell Coleman and Rep. Brett Guthrie had pledged support for a Comer bid in August and on Nov. 2.

The Washington Examiner reported that Comer enters the Republican primary as the front-runner. He had spent months teasing a run and had indicated he would launch it shortly after the midterms.

Three other Republicans have indicated in Kentucky Registry of Election Finance filings that they plan to run. They are Rick Hardin of Leitchfield, Brett St. Amand of Lexington and Charles “Bruiser” Martin of London. Hardin is a state attorney, while Martin is a former reality TV contestant.

Two Democrats are running. Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman has served throughout Beshear’s tenure. Rocky Adkins, a longtime former state House leader, was Beshear’s senior adviser for more than six years.

Comer, 54, grew up in Tompkinsville, Kentucky, and graduated from Western Kentucky University. He served in the Kentucky House from 2001 to 2011, then spent one four-year term as state agriculture commissioner.

He has represented Kentucky’s 1st Congressional District since November 2016, when he won a special election to replace Rep. Ed Whitfield, who resigned. Comer has chaired Oversight since Republicans regained the House majority in 2023. Fox News reported that his investigations included the federal government’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case and former President Joe Biden’s use of an autopen.

It was not immediately known whether Comer will retain his House seat and committee chairmanship during the campaign.

Kentucky’s primary elections are scheduled for May 18, followed by the general election on Nov. 2.
news.summary: The Republican House Oversight chair says eliminating Kentucky's income tax would be his top priority as governor.
news.author: Inquisitr Politics Desk

news.title: How a Black Democrat Survived Redistricting in Alabama
news.text:
Warren Tidwell is glad the election is over. 

Tidwell, a community organizer, recognizes there was a sea change on election night. 

“They say it was a blue wave,” Tidwell said. “Or a blue tsunami.”

But he’s tired of the water metaphors. 

For weeks, Tidwell had been working to help organize disaster relief across the rural Alabama counties that stretch atop the Florida panhandle. Because of the rains and winds of Hurricane Isaias, which hit Alabama last month, he’s seen enough water damage for a lifetime. So for him, the analogies fall flat. 

And for the residents he’s been helping, the election wasn’t a political game, he said. It was a cry for help. 

In Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, which includes many of the impacted counties, voters bucked state Republicans’ attempt to oust U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, a Black Democratic incumbent they had drawn out of his own district earlier this year. That move came after President Donald Trump called for redistricting in red states, and the Supreme Court ruled that the Voting Rights Act does not require the creation of majority-minority congressional districts to facilitate the election of minority voters’ candidates of choice.

Figures, running in the new, heavily Republican district, outperformed all expectations, defeating his Trump-endorsed opponent, Rhett Marques, by more than 7 points. Had those new boundaries been in effect during the 2024 presidential election, Donald Trump would have beaten Kamala Harris by 15 points, 57 percent to 42 percent.

“Where is FEMA?”

On Oct. 9, Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Florida Gulf coast around 8:30 p.m. local time, cutting its way across the middle of Alabama, eventually killing nine people across three states and causing billions of dollars in damage. 

On Oct. 24, all of Alabama’s congressional delegation—Republicans and Democrats— signed a letter supporting Gov. Kay Ivey’s request to Trump for a major disaster declaration for 23 counties in the southern part of the state, including much of the second district. They have received no reply. 

Instead, on Oct. 27, Trump issued a major disaster declaration for the 15 Florida counties in the path of the storm. Escambia County, Florida, residents would benefit from a major disaster declaration; residents of neighboring Escambia County, Alabama, still have no word whether they will get help. 

Everywhere Tidwell has travelled across the impacted counties in south Alabama, residents still struggling to meet their basic needs have asked him the same question: “Where is FEMA?”

Tidwell, who serves as executive director of the Alabama Center for Rural Organizing and Systemic Solutions, said many voters likely had that question in mind on election day. But disaster relief shouldn’t be about political affiliation, he said. 

“If someone asks me who these people voted for, I’ll scream,” he said. “These people need help, not a campaign promise.”

Pastor Timothy Williams, a resident of the historically Black Shiloh community in Coffee County, said voters living in the district were already tired of high prices and low wages before the hurricane. In its wake, Williams said, neighbors have had to rely on each other, not the federal government, to recover from the storm. 

“We haven’t seen much of any federal response,” Williams said. “The hurricane split light poles. It took trees. It damaged people’s roofs.” 

Williams’ family evacuated to a local motel during the storm instead of hunkering down in their home, which has repeatedly faced flooding since a 2018 highway expansion. 

Andrea Eckelman, a political science professor at the University of Montevallo, Alabama’s public liberal arts college, said that issues like disaster relief can compel voters to the polls for a very good reason.

“That’s the point at which it all starts to feel personal,” Eckelman said. “You may be able to explain away high prices for a while, but you can’t explain away why the family whose home has been destroyed isn’t getting help.”

Sources familiar with Ivey and Trump’s relationship told Inside Climate News that Trump’s delayed decision on a major disaster declaration for Alabama in the wake of Isaias stems from his icy relationship with the state’s governor, which began with the denial of Trump’s request to hold a political rally in 2021 onboard the U.S.S. Alabama, a battleship docked in Mobile Bay. Ivey denied any involvement in the decision to reject Trump’s request at the time. 

In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied that Trump’s decisions regarding disaster relief are motivated by politics. 

“The President responds to each request for Federal assistance under the Stafford Act with great care and consideration, ensuring American tax dollars are used appropriately and efficiently by the states to supplement—not substitute, their obligation to respond to and recover from disasters,” Bis wrote. “There is no politicization to the President’s decisions on disaster relief.” 

In an interview Monday, Rep. Figures said that he hopes the president isn’t playing politics with disaster relief decisions but that he wouldn’t be surprised. 

“Nothing would surprise me with this president and how petty [the White House] can be in terms of decisions they make—even decisions as basic as getting disaster relief to impacted communities,” Figures said. 

Figures’ first speech on the House floor in 2025 urged federal relief for California in the wake of the state’s historic wildfires.

“I still don’t know that they’ve received adequate aid like they would have gotten under a normal presidency, Democrat or Republican,” he said. 

As he fed his fussy one-year-old—his “fourth and final” child—Figures told Inside Climate News that Alabama’s congressional delegation and Gov. Ivey have done everything they can to secure a major disaster declaration.

“One would think that we’d be able to get a response quickly and go ahead and get resources down to the people who actually need it, but unfortunately that hasn’t happened yet,” Figures said. “But we’re going to keep pushing.”

Figures said that those most heavily impacted by the storm in Alabama are in areas of his former district now represented by U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, also a Democrat, and that regardless of district lines, all Alabamians deserve access to disaster relief regardless of their politics. 

“Some of these are very rural communities with high levels of poverty and not a lot of infrastructure and certainly not a lot of local resources to respond to a major disaster like this,” he said. “So we need federal aid. We need it in those communities, regardless of whether they’re in my district or not. Those communities still need the federal government to be there when they need them most.” 

There’s a lesson to be learned here, Figures said. People need help from their government regardless of what voting district they’ve been placed into for political reasons. And those decisions—politicans choosing voters instead of the other way around—can ultimately have unexpected consequences at the ballot box.

Steve Flowers, a veteran GOP political commentator and former state House member, said that in the end, Republicans will have to realize that redistricting ultimately backfired, even in Alabama. Instead of creating new safe seats for Republicans, the redistricting drove Black voters to the polls in areas of the state where turnout has lagged for decades. That had impacts on election results, he said. Alabama may not have experienced a blue tsunami. But it got wet.

“It was probably a bad idea for Republicans,” Flowers said, “And Figures benefited from the blue wave across the nation, too.” 

Flowers acknowledged that Republicans in the state had tried their best to boot Figures from Congress in the wake of a U.S. Supreme Court decision further diminishing the Voting Rights Act. 

“They wanted to destroy his district,” Flowers said of state Republicans. 

Instead of “destroying the district,” the GOP plan drove Black turnout. Figures won more votes in majority-Black Montgomery County in the midterm election than he had in the last presidential cycle. 

Alabama Republicans knew Shomari Figures is a Mobile man. 

His father, civil rights attorney Michael Figures, had helped bankrupt the Klan in the wake of the 1981 lynching of Michael Donald, a black teenager, in the state’s port city. His mother has represented Mobile in the state Senate for years, championing air quality reforms while cheering on her son, who worked at the U.S. Department of Justice before his tenure in Congress. 

So when the state GOP went to the drawing board, they knew what they were doing, Flowers said. State Republicans, emboldened by the national push to redistrict, placed Figures in a district that didn’t include Mobile, his hometown and incorporated areas of the predominantly white Wiregrass in the far southeastern part of the state. 

“I don’t think it’s a secret,” Figures said Monday. “They were hoping to get rid of me and then probably take steps in the next session to try and get rid of [Congresswoman] Sewell, too.”

But Republicans’ plan to isolate Figures and move the state one step closer to an all-Republican congressional delegation didn’t quite work. 

Figures moved to Montgomery and mounted an aggressive campaign to retain his seat—a campaign focused on affordability, agriculture and improving rural access to health care. It would be a winning combination. 

A Blue Win in Deep Red Alabama

Figures said unlike some national pundits, he wasn’t surprised by the election results. 

“A lot of these national race raters and experts have never spent a day in Alabama,” Figures said. “They’ve never worked a race in Alabama. They don’t even have friends or family in Alabama. They just look at numbers on a screen.”

But Figures and his team knew what was happening on the ground in the district for one simple reason: They were actually there, listening to voters.

“They’re tired of the breakdown in decency. Tired of the breakdown in norms. Tired of being lied to by the government, particularly by the White House. ‘I’m going to lower prices on day one.’ Did not happen. ‘I’m not getting into forever wars.’ Did not happen. ‘I’m going to release the Epstein Files.’ Did not happen.”

Another clear factor? 

“Gas prices, gas prices, gas prices,” Figures said. “And they’re high right now because of an optional war that we are in in Iran.”

The war has also impacted farmers in Figures’ district as fertilizer prices spike as a result of shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. 

Eckelman, the Montevallo political science professor, said that some of the fragile coalitions that provided the GOP such decisive victories in the past have also begun to erode, even in places in Alabama considered deep Trump country. And while Alabama didn’t see Democrats take any major offices statewide, Eckelman said that victories like Figures’ will serve as examples of what a winning Democratic campaign in a Republican state could look like. 

“The national media and the national Democratic Party may not pay much attention to Alabama, but things are happening here,” Eckelman said. The state’s Democratic Party infrastructure, for example, is improving for the first time in decades, and the party is able to recruit better candidates up and down the ticket, she said. 

Former U.S. Sen. Doug Jones was the party’s nominee for governor, coming within four points of Sen. Tommy Tuberville, a Republican and former Auburn football coach, in the race for governor, the closest margin for the office in decades. Figures called Alabama’s gubernatorial race the largest swing to the left in the country, despite the outcome. 

Down the line, Figures and Sewell may have to deal with efforts to again redraw district lines to oust them from congress. But for now, said David A. Hughes, a political scientist at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette who studies Alabama politics, progressives in the state can rest assured that Democrats in Alabama did better on Nov. 3 than they have in years.

“Go look at the election map of Alabama,” Hughes said. “All 67 counties shifted toward the Democratic side compared to the last election. That’s saying something.”

Figures agreed.

“There’s hope,” he said. “There’s a lot of work to be done, but we’ve made significant strides. And I do think there’s more on the horizon.”

news.title: Republicans Won Fewer Than Half of Trump’s Gen Z Voters in Midterms—Poll
news.text: Fewer than half of Gen Z voters who cast their ballots for President Donald Trump in the 2024 election backed Republicans in the 2026 midterm elections, according to a new J.L. Partners post-midterm poll. Republicans lost more ground among Gen Z than any other age group, with only 42 percent of Gen Z voters who supported Trump heading to the polls to vote for Republican candidates this year, the poll found. While some of these voters backed Democrats this time around, the major shift was due to a collapse in turnout. Sixteen percent of Gen Z Trump voters supported Democratic candidates this year, while 34 percent did not vote, according to the poll. It surveyed 1,000 registered voters on Election Day and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. The new data come as Republicans continue to grapple with difficult midterm election results. Democrats won comfortable majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate in an environment defined by Trump’s declining national approval rating and frustration over the state of the economy and gas prices. Democrats saw gains across demographic groups, but the Gen Z shift is especially notable because young voters shifted toward Trump from 2020 to 2024, helping propel his victory over former Vice President Kamala Harris, defying their reputation as being one of the most progressive voting blocs. Two years later, Trump’s gains among the youngest voters in the country have appeared to evaporate, with the poll suggesting Republicans have struggled to replicate Trump’s success with Gen Z voters. Newsweek reached out to the Republican National Committee (RNC) for comment via email. Where Republicans Lost Votes—What Poll Shows Gen Z was the age group that saw the most significant defections from Trump in this year’s midterms, the poll found. But the poll also found that Hispanic Trump voters shifted away from the GOP. It found that only 37 percent of Hispanic Trump 2024 voters cast their ballots for Republicans this year, compared to 7 percent who supported Democrats and 46 percent who simply stayed home. Democrats did particularly well in places with a high concentration of Hispanic voters. They nearly flipped two House seats in South Florida and swept statewide races in Arizona and Nevada, two swing states that narrowly backed Trump two years earlier. But the shift was especially important in Texas, a traditionally conservative state that Democrats flipped this year. Democrats won the Senate race, governorship and several other statewide offices. They also won back voters in South Texas, a former Democratic stronghold that shifted toward Trump in 2024. In total, 52 percent of Trump’s 2024 voters cast their ballots for Republican candidates, the poll found. Eight percent voted for Democrats, while 35 percent stayed home during the midterms. How Did Gen Z Vote in 2024? Voters between the ages of 18 and 29 shifted rightward from 2020 to 2024, backing Harris by only an 11-point margin, 54 percent to 43 percent, according to CNN exit polling data. Former President Joe Biden won that age group by 24 points in 2020, while former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton won them by 19 points in 2016, exit polling data found. How Did Gen Z Vote in the Midterms? Gen Z shifted significantly leftward in the 2026 midterms, backing Democrats by 50 points, 74 percent to 24 percent, according to CNN exit polling. They backed Democrats by a larger margin than any other age group. Democrats won voters between 30 and 44 by 28 points, voters between 45 and 64 by 7 points and those 65 and older by a single point, according to exit polling data. Trump’s approval rating had fallen with all groups, but especially with Gen Z voters. Recent polling from YouGov and The Economist, conducted from November 4 to 6 among 3,166 registered voters, found that only 30 percent of 18 to 29-year-olds approved of Trump, compared to 66 percent of whom disapproved of him. Young voters comprise a modest share of the electorate—about 11 percent, according to exit polling data—but those shifts contributed to Democrats’ blue tsunami that carried them to victory across the country. Gen Z voters proved important in several key races. In the Texas Senate race, where Democratic Senator-elect James Talarico defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton by about 12 points, Gen Z backed Talarico by 60 points, 79 percent to 19 percent, according to exit polls. Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed won voters between 18 and 29 by a 41-point margin against Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate race, 69 percent to 28 percent, helping contribute to his 7-point statewide win. Meanwhile, Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, won 18-29 voters by 72 points, 85 percent to 13 percent, over Republican Mike Collins in his reelection bid. Only 9 percent of voters between the ages of 18 and 29 considered themselves to be MAGA, while 34 percent said they would describe themselves as a democratic socialist, according to the CNN exit poll data. Forty-nine percent said they’re liberal, 31 percent described themselves as moderate, while only 20 percent said they were conservative. Dissatisfaction with Trump and the economy may have fueled Republicans’ collapse with young voters. Most of those voters—83 percent—said they disapproved of Trump, with only 17 percent saying they approved of him on Election Day. The economy was a major driving factor for Gen Z, with 93 percent describing the cost of living as being crucial or major in deciding their vote. Seventy percent also said the Iran war was crucial or major in deciding their vote, the polling found. House and Senate Election Results 2026 Nearly two weeks after the midterms, the majority of House and Senate races have been called by the Associated Press. As of Monday, Democrats were projected to hold 256 seats in the House, compared to Republicans’ 170 seats. In the Senate, the AP projected 55 seats going to Democrats with 44 seats going to Republicans. Which Races Are Still Undecided? Some races were still uncalled Monday evening. The most prominent uncalled race was the Alaska Senate contest, where Democrat Mary Peltola, a former representative, led GOP Senator Dan Sullivan by nearly 4 points—49.9 percent to 46 percent. If no candidate reaches an outright majority, the race would go to ranked choice. The following House races also remained uncalled. Furthermore, two Louisiana House races will head to a runoff, with no candidate receiving a majority. Republicans are seen as having an advantage in both races. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Republicans struggled to replicate Trump's inroads with the nation's youngest voters, a new poll found.

news.title: Julian Epstein: “I Don’t Think AOC Is A Serious Candidate”
news.text:
Full Interview:

Full Transcript:

Guy Benson: Well, we’re joined now by Julian Epstein, who was chief counsel to the House Judiciary Committee and a staff director to the House Oversight Committee under the Democrats in the late 90s and early 2000s. Julian, good to have you back here.

Julian Epstein: Hey Guy, it’s a pleasure being with you always. I always tend to learn something from you watching you on Fox and in our discussion. So it’s great to be back.

Guy Benson: That’s very kind of you to say and we like having you here as well, although we kind of have to talk through what happened two weeks ago tomorrow and commiserate a bit. I know that you were very concerned about the direction of your political party. Some of the races in particular were of great interest to you. We talked a lot about Michigan, the Senate race there, and that race, like almost all of them–basically every competitive race, and then some that didn’t seem competitive then became competitive–went one direction in this washout blue wave tsunami situation. And now you’ve got a party with enormous governing majorities in Congress at least coming into play starting in January, and I think you’ve got a lot of people now jockeying for sort of positions of power into the future, whether in leadership or at the presidential level, or really trying to influence which wing or part of the party ends up on top and kind of supreme. And there’s a lot of battles playing out right now for that control, and one of the proxy fights is this Chuck Schumer majority leader question. He says he’s got the votes. I’ve seen reporting that he’s got the votes; he just needs a majority of the incoming caucus to become majority leader. We’ve got this Chris Van Hollen from Maryland who is his challenger. He says that’s nonsense and he’s going to be fighting this thing out. He, of course, has been pandering hard to the progressive wing, the left-wingers on Israel. He’s turned sharply against Israel. He’s gone to bat for criminal illegal immigrants. He’s kind of gone, you know, face-first in the tank for the whole left-wing agenda. So that’s one of these battles that’s already brewing. How do you read it? And if in fact you do believe that Schumer’s fine, he’ll be fine and be elected, what kind of leash will he have? Because I know the base, right? The base reviles him.

Julian Epstein: Yeah, I think that’s the right question, Guy, and thanks again for having me on. I think the news media is missing what’s going on here. They’re treating this as a horse race, and it’s not a horse race–it’s a flex. It’s a flex by the progressives and the socialists in the party, and Schumer does have the votes. He’s probably got 29, which is the amount of votes that he needs.

Guy Benson: Some of the numbers have it higher and into like the upper 30s even, so we’ll see.

Julian Epstein: Yeah, what Van Hollen is trying to do on behalf of the socialists and the hard leftists is to tell Schumer that the caucus is divided and that if he wants to get anything done, Schumer is going to have to capitulate. He’s going to have to make major concessions to the hard left. Now, what those concessions are is yet to be determined. You’ve got people like Ron Wyden, who’s talking about spending $8 or $10 million–$8 to $10 trillion–on new tax-and-spend welfare spending. You’ve got a big portion of the Democratic caucus that wants to isolate Israel and take away its ability for self-defense in what is a war against fascism in the Middle East. You’ve sort of got the Green New Deal agenda that’s trying to be revived by the socialists. It’s not clear what exactly Van Hollen would do on behalf of the socialists and the hard left, but what he’s saying is, “I’ve got a group of 15, 20 senators who, if you want to get anything done, you’re going to have to capitulate to them.” And that’s what this is about.

Guy Benson: Medicare for All also being, you know, one of these demands you’re seeing creeping up on the left.

Julian Epstein: I tell you, that’s a con job. I don’t even think they’re going to bring Medicare for All up for a vote, because they tried to do this, I think it was 2019. And as soon as voters realize that it’s going to mean an end to their employer-based insurance and substitute it for a very lousy form of government-run insurance, the numbers turn immediately. They go, let’s say, 80-20 against it. And the Democrats know that this whole Medicare for All campaign slogan was a complete con job. I would bet a dollar to a donut that it never comes up for a vote.

Guy Benson: I think it may not come up for a vote in the upcoming Congress. I think they want to keep the idea alive, get the trifecta, and then do a lot of things if they can, including Medicare for All, but that’s–

Julian Epstein: Well, it’s grandstanding. It’s grandstanding, this demagoguery. They hope that the public doesn’t look at this the way they hope the public doesn’t look at the rest of what’s going on. I mean, the federal government is functionally insolvent right now. We’re $40 trillion in debt with $2 trillion every year adding on to that. We, you know, we are going in the direction of France very, very slowly, but surely. And you know, you look at the con job that’s being told by a welfare state that continues to fail. Obamacare was supposed to solve the problem for the uninsured and the underinsured, right? And what Obamacare has done is it’s killed competition, it’s increased consolidation, and it’s basically been a blank check for insurance companies.

Guy Benson: Well, and premiums keep going up. I saw there was like a double-digit premium increase this year under the quote-unquote Affordable Care Act, which is the last time Democrats–

Julian Epstein: They’re expecting 14%–I think the number is somewhere between 12 and 14%. But it stands to reason that this would happen, because basically what the federal government is saying to insurance companies is, “Charge whatever you like for the most part, and the consumer, the patient is only going to have to pay a small fraction of those costs, and the government will pay the rest.” And so it’s a blank check for insurance companies. And it was very foreseeable. Conservatives pointed that out at the time, but not loudly enough. I mean, the conservative message machine here during the midterms and even now is just horrible.

Guy Benson: I mean, I do think, in fairness, I do think conservatives won the argument on Obamacare and won huge majorities to try to stop it in 2010. But it was too late. Democrats jammed it through anyway. And I think they would love to do the same with a government takeover of health care if they have the votes–probably not again in the next two years, but thereafter, if they had all of those levers of power. But I just want to come back, because the Van Hollen thing, you’re calling it a flex. I started to identify him as someone with clear national ambitions the moment he started really turning on Israel, because that’s kind of the spirit of the base of the party right now, where you cannot go anywhere in national Democratic politics unless you are foaming at the mouth about the Jewish state. And then, you know, his stunt going down and having whatever the margaritas with the criminal alien, all of that. He is pandering to that very sizable base. They feel emboldened, and I know that the more moderate folks are saying, “Look, without us, we don’t have these big majorities.” I don’t think that the left-wingers care. I think the left-wingers are like, “We’ve got these majorities. We’ve shown that we can win even in a place like Michigan, and now we’ve got to govern like left-wing socialists, and if you’re not going to do it, you’re going to have big, big problems.” I feel like the Dems are going to have lots of wiggle room, right? Margin for error given the size of these majorities, but there are some underlying tensions that could bubble to the surface, especially in an upcoming presidential primary where you’re going to have a lot of people running that hard-left route to try to get to the White House and saying, “Listen, we can win. It doesn’t matter what we believe in, what we say. 2026 proves that this stuff can win nationwide.” And are they wrong?

Julian Epstein: Yeah, they’re wrong. And they’re wrong. I mean, the Democratic Party, Guy, continues to be 10 points behind the Republican Party in terms of public favorability and brand favorability.

Guy Benson: Yeah, they just won 56 Senate seats and 260 House seats, though.

Julian Epstein: That’s not because anything they’re doing is popular. That’s because people were repulsed by what Trump is doing, which is he is spending too much time on vanity projects and not enough time on a plan for the future. And he was god-awful in terms of explaining what was a very noble undertaking in Iran. This is something that has to be explained to the public, which wasn’t, except for these one-offs. And it was a rejection of Trump. It was not any kind of mandate or validation of what the Democrats were arguing. news.title: Opinion: What next? Euphoria over U.S. midterms fades under trade policy reality checks
news.text:
Article content

In the days before the recent U.S. midterm elections, we were treated to mixed trade messages. U.S. President Donald Trump told Fox News, “We’re going to make a deal with Canada very soon. We’re going to make a great deal.” Meanwhile, on the U.S. news outlet Politico, Prime Minister Mark Carney ‌said, “Canada is prepared to wait until a new U.S. president takes office rather than rush into a trade agreement under unfavourable terms with U.S. President Trump.”

It is clear that trade negotiations had been intensifying over the past weeks. What has been less clear is where this is leading us. In the wake of midterm results, two distinct options seem to be emerging for Canada. One argues that Canada should try to land an acceptable trade deal now given that the Trump administration is on the ropes. Another suggests Canada should wait out the rest of Trump’s term and resume negotiations with a new administration that might be more supportive of the spirit and letter of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico trade agreement (CUSMA). If posed as hockey analogies, what would we choose: “sudden death overtime” or “ragging the puck”? The answer is — it depends. It depends on what version of the Democratic party shows up to take over Congress in January.

Recommended Videos

Both options assume that a Democrat-controlled Congress will clip Trump’s protectionist wings and force a rollback of his waves of tariffs. Affordability was the defining domestic issue in the midterms. In a September survey, the U.S.-based Cato Institute found that 75 per cent of respondents thought Trump’s tariffs had increased domestic household prices. Over half thought the tariffs had weakened the U.S. economy. On Nov. 3, the ballot box delivered a pretty clear mandate for Democrats to address affordability challenges like tariffs. What is not clear is exactly how they intend to act and whether they can restrain Trump’s exercise of executive authority under which all of his extraordinary tariffs have been invoked.

Before examining this, let’s set the stage with a brief recap on where we’re at on tariffs and trade talks.

Trump’s tariffs have descended on Canada in waves over the past two years — with the largest delivering sectoral tariffs ranging from 10 per cent to 50 per cent on our exports of softwood lumber, autos, steel and aluminum. Some earlier tariffs have been struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court only to be replaced by tariffs invoked under other emergency authorities allegedly within the president’s ambit. In August, Trump imposed tariffs of up to 50 per cent on $27.6 billion of Canadian exports. Canada reciprocated in September with dollar-for-dollar tariffs on a range of U.S. exports. Since then, both countries have switched up their hit lists, adding products in, taking others out. Trump has said he would increase current sectoral tariffs on automobiles and steel to 50 per cent on Jan. 1, but nothing has been seen on this beyond a Truth Social post.

Canada remains the only country outside of China that is actively retaliating against U.S. tariffs. Yet, through all of this, CUSMA remains in place. The U.S. has not given Canada and Mexico the required six-month notice of its intent to withdraw from the treaty. So, surprisingly, despite rounds of retaliation, CUSMA still affords duty-free treatment to over 80 per cent of Canada’s exports to the U.S. Is your head spinning yet?

Now, enter the Democrats and with them our hopes that they will bring saner heads to prevail. But can we count on them to return us to a CUSMA free-trade environment?

Historically, the Democrats have not been flag-carriers for free trade. Canada’s free-trade pacts with the U.S. have all been negotiated by Republican administrations. In January 2020, CUSMA was approved by the U.S. Senate by a vote of 89 to 10. Of the “nays,” eight were Democrats, including party heavyweights such as current Senate Minority leader Chuck Schumer, Senator Cory Booker and then-Senator, later vice-president and presidential nominee, Kamala Harris. With respect to B.C.’s largest trade battle with the U.S., it should be noted that the current 35 per cent tariff on softwood lumber exports was initiated under Democratic President Joe Biden. Trump added a 10 per cent top-up as an alleged “national security” measure.

A large part of Trump’s road to victory over the past few elections has been through swing states in the U.S. rust belt where the Republicans have taken labour voters away from the Democrats. The Democrats will be fighting to get those once-loyal voters back. There is little that these voters like more than a journey to the past aided by some good old America-first protectionism. Such measures should block imports without increasing prices — as Trump’s tariffs on Canadian aluminum have on beer cans.

Several of the new representatives are heading to Congress under the fledgling wing of the Democratic Socialist movement. While this cohort has yet to define a distinct political platform, I would bet that free trade with Canada and Mexico is not going to be a priority in its anti-globalization agenda.

While Congressional election results are dramatic and clear, the path for a Democratic-controlled Congress to revoke Trump’s tariffs is less so. These tariffs have all been invoked under presidential authorities to take emergency action without any recourse to Congress. Some of these tariffs have been struck down by courts as unwarranted extensions of these emergency powers. Throughout waves of tariffs, the current Democratic minority in Congress has meekly asserted that tariffs are taxes and that Congress alone has the authority to raise taxes. But to no avail. Now that the tables have turned in Congress, it is still unclear how the Democrats will unstick this issue. Drafting legislation to promote affordability by revoking Trump’s tariffs will surely run into the president’s veto stamp — soon to replace his signature Sharpie as his favourite desk ornament. Despite their big win, the Democrats are over a dozen seats short of the two-thirds super-majority required in both the House of Representatives and Senate to overturn a presidential veto. Alternatively, the parties may choose the great American tradition of “lawyering up” and taking tariffs to court. Both scenarios threaten paralysis.

So where does this leave Canada? Arguably, we gain leverage when American voters draw a direct line between Trump’s tariffs and cost-of-living affordability. But we’re not in control of how this manifests in action. What is clear though is that Canada cannot count on either Democrats or Republicans to return us to the tariff-free status quo that has prevailed in our bilateral trade over most of the past four decades. Borrowing Carney’s oft-quoted phrase, this is what a “rupture” in our relationship looks like.

It may be prudent to let the dust settle a bit and understand if and how the Democrats plan to act. Continuing to reinforce the connection between tariffs and affordability should be a strong focus. Equally, we should emphasize the impact of tariffs on the economies of U.S. states where Canada is the largest export market — as is now the case in over half of U.S. states, including five out of eight in which Democrats flipped Republican Senate seats in the midterms.

At best, we may hope that the emerging U.S. trade environment will be less chaotic — but it won’t be calm nor more certain. In light of this prospect, one wonders what could provide Canada a bigger incentive to turbo-charge our trade diversification initiatives.

Stuart Culbertson is a former deputy minister in the government of B.C. He served as B.C. Trade Representative during the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement negotiations. He participated in the U.S. State Department’s International Leadership Visitor Program in 1995.

news.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump’s effort to impose DEI policies on UC researchers
news.text:
This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

The Supreme Court rejected the White House’s bid to have the high court review a case that forced the Trump administration to return hundreds of research grants to academics at the University of California.

The court issued the decision today. No justice filed a brief explaining the decision, which is common. 

Lawyers for the U.S. Department of Justice argued that federal agencies had the right to terminate the grants because they ran afoul of the Trump administration’s executive orders on defunding so-called Diversity, Equity and Inclusion efforts, plus research on the effects of global warming. 

But attorneys for the UC researchers depicted that rationale as dangerous to science and to the academics’ constitutional rights. “What begins as material harm – loss of money, staff, graduate and post-doctoral students – quickly becomes expressive harm: the inability to publish research and affect public discourse. This is a quintessential First Amendment violation,” the lawyers for the UC researchers wrote in a legal brief to the high court.

The case is known as Thakur v. Trump and concerns grants on U.S. history, disease research and biology, among many others.Between January and July of last year the White House terminated more than $900 million in grants to UC researchers, including nearly $600 million at UCLA alone. Almost all of those grants were restored after a lower court judge ordered the federal agencies to restore them across multiple court decisions. After the federal government appealed, the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld those decisions that said the White House likely violated the researchers’ First Amendment rights.Agencies terminated the grant funding of researchers through keyword searches of grant applications that used words such as “diversity” or “climate change,” CalMatters previously reported. The Department of Energy cut grants specifically to states that voted for Kamala Harris over Trump in 2024.

Grants issued by the National Institutes of Health also required academics to research a diverse pool of Americans. When the agency terminated a $36 million grant on dementia led by a UC Davis professor in April of last year for focusing on diversity, CalMatters reported that the first Trump administration required a focus on diversity in the grant applications. The National Institutes of Health restored the grant shortly after CalMatters ran its story. 

Some of the research projects the National Science Foundation terminated had nothing to do with diversity and equity initiatives, lawyers for the researchers wrote. They say the foundation targeted grants that included the word “diversity” in describing a scientific approach. Those included projects with titles such as the “Effects of Leaf Diversity on Aquatic Insect Colonizer Diversity” and “Revealing the Vast Diversity Within the Legume-Rhizobia Mutualism.”

Claudia Polsky, a lawyer for the UC researchers, said the Supreme Court’s decision is a boon to similar cases across the country. Lawyers for other researchers whose grants the federal government cancelled are also arguing that the White House violated their First Amendment rights. Those lawyers can point to the fact that the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals agreed with the UC researchers and the Supreme Court rejected the White House’s challenge. Those courts are “not technically bound by anything. But I think they will find it quite persuasive,” Polsky said. She doesn’t think the White House will attempt to appeal again, since the justices showed no dissent in their rejection.She added that this decision directly benefits Cal State professors who sued the Trump administration last month over the termination of National Science Foundation grants.The lawyers for the UC researchers will return to a lower court hearing Tuesday to argue that the Trump administration’s termination of Department of Energy grants were also illegal. That case is technically unrelated to today’s Supreme Court decision.

Legal dispute

A central dispute in the case is determining when the federal government can cancel grant funding. Lawyers for the researchers said that once a grant is awarded to academics — regardless of which administration issued it — the academics should be allowed to complete their research, even if the current administration views the research as a waste of taxpayer money. 

But the Department of Justice was adamant that the federal government can cancel already-funded grants. That’s not a First Amendment violation, the agency argued, because the White House isn’t preventing the researchers from seeking private funding to conduct their research. The UC researchers didn’t break any rules set by Congress in how they carried out their research and complied with detailed guidelines on how to use federal money, the federal agencies affirmed in signed statements this summer. 

But to the Trump administration, that didn’t matter. The agencies terminated the grants anyway because they no longer aligned with the president’s directives.Lawyers for the researchers wrote that the legal precedent argued by the White House would end stability for federal science and humanities research. They argued any project funded for multiple years that extends into the tenure of a new U.S. president would be susceptible to early cancellation. Science cannot operate under that kind of caprice, the lawyers for the researchers argued.

A lower court judge, appointed by Biden, agreed when ordering the agencies to restore the grants. “They face unexpected funding shortfalls, will likely have to lay off staff, and will experience career and reputational harm if they cannot complete their projects. They also must spend time seeking alternate funding, a time-consuming process with little chance of success,” wrote the judge, Rita F. Lin of the U.S. District Court for Northern California.The Department of Justice represented several federal agencies specifically, including the Department of Defense, the Department of Transportation, the National Endowment for the Humanities, the National Institutes of Health, and the National Science Foundation.The lawyers settled with the Environmental Protection Agency over similar issues this year.

Can the White House cancel grants already approved?

Department of Justice lawyers argued that as long as the administration isn’t forcing researchers to adopt the views of the White House in their private affairs, their rights aren’t violated. Lawyers for the researchers blasted that logic. The White House “can point to no case” in which any federal court “has held that the President and federal agencies may terminate grants awarded through a merit-driven competitive process based on the perceived viewpoint of the research,” they wrote in their legal brief urging the Supreme Court to reject the case. 

The legal team for the researchers wrote that the White House is disregarding the processes that Congress established for terminating existing grants. The lawyers for the researchers noted that Congress embedded language in the laws governing the research agencies to encourage research that focused on women, people of color and individuals with disabilities, including at the National Science Foundation. Similar language governs the National Endowment for the Humanities, such as giving “particular regard to scholars, and educational and cultural institutions, that have traditionally been underrepresented.” 

CalMatters is a nonpartisan and nonprofit news organization bringing Californians stories that probe, explain and explore solutions to quality of life issues while holding our leaders accountable.
news.summary: The high court denied an appeal from the Trump administration and ordered it to restore roughly $1 billion in UC research grants.
news.author: Mikhail Zinshteyn • Calmatters

news.title: Furious Trump turns on CBS boss Bari Weiss and Norah O'Donnell as the network gloves come off after midterm defeat
news.text:
Donald Trump hit out at the new leadership of CBS News' 60 Minutes this week after a Sunday segment sought to 'measure the cost of the Iran war.'

Trump, 80, accused CBS Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss and others of spreading misleading information about the state of the conflict in the Norah O'Donnell led-report.

The new piece was based on an eight-month investigation that found glaring US military failures surrounding the deadliest attack against US troops during the war back in March.

O’Donnell, at a point, reported on how military brass allegedly disregarded threats of Iran kamikaze drone attacks and ignored US intelligence that may have saved six American lives.

In a blistering post to Truth Social on Monday morning, the president slammed 'the new people running 60 Minutes' as 'even worse than their predecessors' - a far cry from the praise he heaped on Weiss at the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner in July. 

The president cited several statistics about the war that he said was 'left out of the 60 Minutes "report,"' while insisting 'no one in the world has the ability to do so well' in dealing with the conflict. 

The public criticism comes a week after the conservative made light of Republicans' election losses on the program’s post-midterm elections broadcast. 

Trump insisted in the post on Monday that 'the early stages of Iran was not correctly stated.'

'Since February 28, 2026, the start of Epic Fury, Iran has fired between 8,000-9,000 One-way Attack Drones,' he wrote.

'Only 2 of them got through, resulting in US fatalities, both on the first day, hitting Kuwait and Saudi Arabia.'

'Likewise, Iran has fired about 2,000 Ballistic Missiles. Only 1 out of the 2,0000 got through, and caused U.S. fatalities (Jordan).'

To end the post, Trump gave those keeping track a 'translation': '99.99 percent of Iranian missiles and drones' have either been 'shot down' or not tied to any US deaths, he wrote.

'All of this being left out of the 60 Minutes "report." Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP,' the post concluded.

The Daily Mail had approached CBS News for comment on the president's post.

A CBS insider familiar with the segment slammed the post as 'an attempt to distract ' from 60 Minutes' actual reporting. 

Trump's criticism of Weiss comes months after the president praised the CBS News chief as 'a wonderful woman' whom he wished 'all the best at CBS News' on-stage at the White House Correspondents' Dinner in July.

In an interview with CBS just weeks after Weiss was minted in November of last year, Trump told O'Donnell: 'I don't know [Weiss], but I hear she's a great person.'

Weiss, 42, has helmed the network since October of last year and was hired by then-new Paramount CEO David Ellison. 

The show underwent a shakeup under her in May, during which it replaced its executive producer and three correspondents.

After Scott Pelley's sensational exit from the program in June - in protest of those changes - a former CBS News executive told the Mail that 'arrogance' has 'pervaded' CBS for years, particularly within 60 Minutes.

The source said the newsmagazine is known for an 'unwillingness to change' and an overall sense of 'infallibility.'

The changes created an air of anxiety around the show's season premiere in September.

Trump, meanwhile, already sued 60 Minutes in late 2024 over an interview with then-presidential candidate Kamala Harris that alleged 'deceptive editing practices' on the part of the network. The suit was settled in July of last year.

A merger between CBS News' then-parent company, Paramount, and Ellison's Skydance was approved later that month. 

The Iran war is currently in its ninth month and has been widely pegged as a driving factor in the GOP's midterm election losses.

The Pentagon declined to comment on the piece before it aired Sunday, according to CBS. The report detailed at least 31 Iranian strikes on US military and diplomatic sites across eight countries, for the first time.

Trump's statement did not accuse CBS of making any factual errors.
news.summary: Trump, 80, accused CBS's centrist editor-in-chief and others of spreading misleading material by airing the Norah O'Donnell led-report.
news.author: Alex Hammer,Editor

news.title: Here's How We Stop the Democrats' Scheme to Nuke the Electoral College

Democrats have made it clear they'll use every power grab available to lock in permanent control of the federal government. That means nuking the Electoral College, packing the Supreme Court, and establishing two new blue states. After the midterms, one of those schemes moved much closer to reality.

The plan is the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.

Under the compact, each state agrees to give all its electoral votes to the candidate who wins the most votes nationally (regardless of how its own voters have voted). The compact remains dormant until the members of the compact collectively hold at least 270 electoral votes. At that point, it comes into effect.

Here's why Democrats are suddenly excited.

The compact already has 222 electoral votes, 48 short of the required number. The Dems just took full control of Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin, and Nevada, which together hold 61 electoral votes. If all five of those states join, the Dems would have enough states in the compact to make the 2028 election effectively a national popular-vote contest.

There's some irony here, though: President Donald Trump won the national popular vote in 2024.

Eighteen states and Washington, D.C., have signed on since organizers launched the compact in 2006, and every one of them backed Kamala Harris in 2024. If the compact had been in force, Trump would have won the Electoral College 533-5.

The Democrat Party has literally built a weapon that would have handed its opponent a historic landslide.

Of course the Democrats wouldn’t be going down this route if they thought it wouldn’t work in their favor. In the 2024 election alone, you could have a handful of dubious batches of votes in a few deep blue enclaves, and that would be enough to swing the nation. Get rid of the Electoral College, and you make elections far easier to steal. The people who are pushing for it know precisely what they're doing.

So what happens if Democrats actually pull this off?

Attorney General Todd Blanche has a plan.

On Fox News' Life, Liberty & Levin, host Mark Levin asked Blanche whether he'd take the fight all the way to the Supreme Court if Democrat states tried to sidestep the Constitution with a compact.

“There is no doubt," Blanche told Levin. "And by the way, it shouldn't even need to get to the Supreme Court. It shouldn't get past the District Court."

"But yes, we will take it to the Supreme Court if we have to, because this would be a blatant violation of the Constitution."

Levin went on to explain the stakes for his audience. Under the compact, a state whose voters went red could still be compelled to give its electors to the Democrat. news.title: JD Vance Is MAGA’s Choice for 2028
news.text: Vice President JD Vance is currently MAGA'S choice for the 2028 Republican presidential nominee, according to a new poll taken after the midterm elections. The Economist/YouGov survey puts Vance ahead of Secretary of State Marco Rubio among "Americans who intend to vote in the 2028 Republican presidential primaries," 40 percent backing the vice president and 33 percent Rubio. Among MAGA-identifying Republican voters, Vance's lead increases to 45 percent against Rubio's 35 percent. The poll, conducted November 9–11, and published November 13, surveyed 1,685 adult U.S. citizens and makes Vance the favorite to succeed Trump as the party’s standard bearer. Newsweek contacted the White House via email and online form on Monday for comment. Can Vance Win Beyond The MAGA Base? Vance’s advantage over Rubio highlights his strong connection with the voters most committed to Trump’s political movement. But his position is less commanding among Republicans who do not identify with MAGA. In that group, Vance leads Rubio by just 33 percent to 29 percent. The vice president's strong standing among MAGA voters suggests he could begin a Republican primary campaign with a substantial base of support as the natural contender to replace Trump. But winning a general election means building a much broader coalition. Vance has repeatedly stopped short of confirming whether he will run for president in 2028. Describing himself as a procrastinator when it comes to major life decisions, he admitted that he "hates thinking about it." The vice president indicated he would give the decision more serious consideration after the November midterm elections, adding that "anything could happen." In October, Vance said he believed Trump would endorse him if he entered the race. He has acknowledged that Trump's endorsement could carry significant weight in determining the Republican nominee, although he suggested the president might allow the primary contest to play out. The Electability Question The biggest challenge facing Vance may be his ability to attract voters beyond Trump's core supporters. An August Emerson College poll offered an early warning sign, showing Vance losing hypothetical 2028 matchups against several potential Democratic candidates, including Gavin Newsom, Kamala Harris, Pete Buttigieg and Jon Ossoff. The poll of 1,000 likely voters also found Rubio could perform better than Vance in hypothetical contests against Democratic contenders, including Harris and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. So Rubio could have an advantage when it comes to appealing to a wider range of Americans, including independents and moderate voters who will be essential in a general election. Much depends on the relative influence of the MAGA movement on the party as the election approaches. With the 2028 election still nearly two years away, the matchups offer an early indication of potential vulnerabilities rather than a prediction of the eventual outcome. But, if the race comes down to Vance or Rubio their respective strengths will need to develop beyond their current limits. Neither candidate has secured Trump's endorsement, and the president's influence over the eventual Republican nomination could be decisive. Midterm Setbacks Raise New Questions Vance's presidential ambitions have also come under scrutiny following the Republicans' midterm defeats, with reports suggesting he is reconsidering whether 2028 is the right time to run He has also acknowledged the political fallout of the Iran war, describing it as the biggest factor behind Republicans' losses in the November 3 midterms, which cost the party control of both the House and Senate. In a social media post the following day, he appeared to distance himself from the conflict, prompting speculation that he was seeking to protect his own political future amid growing criticism of the US-Israel-led war. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Daniel Orton and Trevor Davies.
news.summary: The Vice President leads among Trump followers, but doubts remain over his wider electability.

news.title: How Talarico Beat Musk's Millions in Texas: 'Tell a Story, Be Normal'
news.text: During the most hectic stretch of the Texas Senate campaign, a month away from Election Day, Democrat James Talarico came down with the flu and spent nearly two weeks away from public events. Republicans saw an opening in an already difficult race for the GOP. Attorney General Ken Paxton seized on his absence, posting mock missing-person posters of his opponent and tweeting: “Talarico claims he was missing for 13 days because he had the ‘flu.’ Who actually believes that?” His campaign fueled rumors that Talarico had suffered “a full-blown mental Tala-freak-out” and was being held at a mental health facility in Ohio. They also demanded “proof of life.” Billionaire and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who poured at least $224 million into supporting the Republican challenger, also weighed in on his social media platform, writing on X: “The Talarico campaign is hiding something big that voters ought to know about.” But Talarico's response, which several Democratic operatives praised as an example of how to handle an increasingly hostile campaign, was not to engage with the attacks. His message was simple: “You have to tell a story, be normal,” Andrew Mamo, lead strategist for Talarico's U.S. Senate campaign, said. “When they went crazy and made up completely insane things about how he was in a mental hospital in Ohio, which he simply was not, we were just normal. We said he's sick, people get sick, he'll be back in a day or two,” Mamo told Newsweek in an interview. The rumor fell apart within hours. The facility, the Lindner Center of Hope in Mason, Ohio, posted that Talarico “has never received treatment” there. Talarico shared the statement and added: “I’ve never even been to Ohio.” By then he was already back in public, appearing at the Austin City Limits Music Festival on October 9. Weeks later, Talarico defeated Paxton by 12 points, delivering Democrats their first Texas Senate victory in 38 years. Newsweek contacted Paxton’s Senate campaign via email on Monday for comment. An Early Story The campaign had prepared for an attack like this one long before Talarico got sick. Mamo said the plan was to introduce Talarico to voters early with positive television ads, then carry the same message across Instagram, TikTok and campaign events. “Being early and positive, because we knew the Republicans were going to come in late and negative and say, 'Actually, this guy is a crazy person,'" he said. “But when you’ve seen James talk about his faith and talk about his family and his career as a teacher, when they say he’s a crazy person, you say, 'No, he’s not. I’ve seen [him] talk. He seems pretty reasonable to me.'” Mamo, who met Talarico in 2021, said the message had been years in the making. A former public school teacher, Talarico has long argued that the country's divide is between the powerful and everyone else, not between political parties. As a state representative, he was also a regular commentator on Fox News where he once had an exchange with then-host Pete Hegseth that later went viral. “Great campaigns have a story to tell, and they tell them from the first day to the last day, and they set the narrative of the race,” Mamo said. That story received an unexpected national boost in February, when Talarico's appearance on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert became a story of its own. Colbert told his audience that CBS would not allow him to interview the Texas Senate candidate because of concerns about the federal government's equal time rule. Colbert posted the conversation on YouTube instead. By February 18, the interview had drawn 85 million views across YouTube and social media. Talarico also raised more than $2.5 million in the 24 hours after the interview moved from CBS to YouTube, which he called the campaign's largest single-day fundraising haul. “When you're watching something and you have the ability to scroll past it, you're actually paying attention because you're deciding to pay attention,” Mamo said, stating that the value of reaching people who actively choose to listen paid off. “The more you can maximize free, opt-in attention, the more money you can spend elsewhere. Getting people to actually care about what you’re saying is the ultimate goal, and I think James did a really great job of that,” Mamo added. Answering the Culture War Republicans spent much of the race trying to put Talarico on the defensive over gender and faith. The line they returned to most came from 2021, when Talarico, a seminarian and aspiring Presbyterian minister, said on the Texas House floor: “God is nonbinary.” Talarico was hardly the only target. Republicans spent an estimated $183 million on television ads focused on transgender-related attacks against Democrats in the final phase of this year’s midterm elections, according to AdImpact data. Mamo said the campaign never dodged those fights. “It’s not that we didn’t engage, because James has always been clear about his values, and the fact that his values haven’t changed from the day he got elected in 2018 to now,” he said. “When they attacked trans kids’ rights, James said, 'No, I will always stand up against anyone trying to bully kids.'” The next step was to widen the conversation. Mamo described it as “almost using their attack energy against them to reroute the conversation to what people really care about.” Many Democrats still remember the final stretch of the 2024 presidential campaign when Donald Trump and his allies leaned heavily on cultural issues to attack then-Vice President Kamala Harris. The “Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you” ad became one of the defining messages of that effort. Democrats were left wary of engaging in cultural fights they believed they were unlikely to win. Mamo said Talarico's campaign took a different approach. Rather than dismissing voters' concerns about cultural issues, it acknowledged them while trying to connect those concerns to what he called “the underlying structural rot” behind their problems. That meant not telling voters that their feelings did not matter or that they were wrong to worry about their children or fairness in sports. “It's totally fair to feel that way, but let's talk about what's really going on,” he said. “I think that turned into a powerful antidote.” The midterms delivered a clear message. Voters cared more about the cost of living than the culture wars the GOP was relying on. That was true in Texas and across the country. About nine in 10 voters said the cost of living was a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote for Congress, according to the AP Voter Poll, a survey of roughly 100,000 midterm voters. About two-thirds said Trump's policies had fueled inflation. Only about one in 10 named immigration or health care as the country's top issue, while even fewer cited foreign policy or crime. Running Against the Richest Man in the World Talarico’s race became the most expensive Senate contest in American history. AdImpact found it was also the most expensive non-presidential race in U.S. history, with $573.2 million in ad spending, much of the money against him coming from Musk. Talarico, meanwhile, built his war chest from donors. He outpaced Paxton in campaign funding, raising $155 million to Paxton’s $40 million. Through the summer, 51 percent of his total fundraising came from individuals who had contributed less than $200, while 88 percent of Paxton’s contributions came from larger donors. Mamo said the outside money mattered less because the campaign had already defined the race. “When you run up against the richest person in the world, you have set the tone and the conversation of the race, and you can win the big conversation, and that turns into results,” he said. Musk and his active involvement in the race became part of Talarico’s message. Democrats won in part by hammering Musk, the tax breaks and grants his companies receive, and his relationships with elected Republicans. Slightly more than half of Texas voters said they had an unfavorable opinion of Musk, according to the AP Voter Poll of more than 5,000 voters in the state. “No matter how much money is spent against you, people know what the race is about, because you’ve decided what the race is about. That is tremendously powerful,” he said. He also argued that a dollar spent on an attack ad buys less than it used to. “When Republicans pay for you to watch an attack ad, that costs money,” Mamo said. “And you’re probably half paying attention to an ad because they’re making you watch it.” Mamo said the goal was to tell “one coherent story across every platform, whether it’s Instagram or TikTok or a television ad or a speech.” “It’s consistency, and it’s being different from everybody else and interesting,” he added. Earning the Latino Vote The campaign’s other priority was Latino voters, who had swung hard toward Republicans two years earlier. Trump captured an estimated 55 percent of the voter bloc in Texas in 2024, which set a new high-water mark for Texas Republicans. Mamo said the campaign did not assume Trump’s immigration crackdown would bring those voters back on its own. Instead, it treated them “as the persuasion voters they are.” “We showed up early in the primary in South Texas over and over again, trying to earn people’s votes and being very clear that we are working to earn their votes,” he said. He recalled riding with the campaign in a parade in Brownsville during the primary, on the back of a pickup truck, while “people were going wild for James Talarico.” Many of the Latino voters the campaign met described themselves as up for grabs. “So many Latino folks we talked to said, 'I am a free agent. I would like to see both sides tell me how they can make my life better, and then I’ll make up my mind,'” Mamo said. The campaign spent “millions and millions of dollars of Spanish-language advertising across TV, digital, you name it,” he said. He added that Talarico’s background as a teacher and his focus on education also resonated with Latino families. The effort paid off. The AP Voter Poll found roughly six in 10 Hispanic voters in Texas supported Talarico, compared with about three in 10 who backed Paxton. Mamo said the result reflected a full-ticket effort that included Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and South Texas House candidates such as Bobby Pulido. The pitch to Latino voters was direct, he said: “You might not have seen yourself as a Democrat two years ago. You might not see yourself as a Democrat today. But here is a group of people who are really sincere about trying to earn your vote and then work to make your life better. Come on board.” A Model or a Protest Vote? Talarico had pitched his campaign as a template long before Election Day. After his primary win in March, The New York Times reported that whether or not he became the next senator from Texas, Talarico believed his campaign could be a model for Democrats across the country as they try to find their way out of their political wilderness. Mamo argues the result proves it. “I think Texas is on the presidential 2028 map. I think it’s a swing state,” he said. “We just proved the question of is it a swing state? Well, it just swung.” Republicans see a more complicated picture. Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican strategist in Texas, said the biggest factor was the national environment and how voters saw Trump’s policies. “The issues nationally weighed on everybody. And it dragged everybody down,” Steinhauser told Newsweek. “I think that’s the most important story from the election.” He ranked problems with Paxton’s candidacy second, still giving Talarico credit: “Talarico did run a good campaign. He knew that he had to appeal to moderates, independents, some Republicans to try and convince them to give him a chance.” “I think they ran a smart campaign,” Steinhauser said. “And I think they showed that the strategy [was] sound and he ended up winning big.” National polling supports the caution. The AP Voter Poll found that while Democrats have at least a slight advantage on several major issues, including the economy and government corruption, the Democratic Party is not much more popular among U.S. voters than the Republican Party. According to the poll, just under half of voters have a "somewhat" or "strongly" favorable view of the Democratic Party, while about four in 10 view the GOP positively. For Mamo, the lesson is about who the party nominates. “There is nothing more important than candidate quality,” he said. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Samantha Beech and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: Talarico’s lead strategist tells Newsweek how staying “normal,” early ads and a Latino push beat Paxton and Musk’s money in Texas.

news.title: Joe Biden Says He's Mending His Relationship With Nancy Pelosi After Bitter Fallout Over His 2024 Election Exit: 'We Had Been Through Too Much Together'
news.text:
Former President Joe Biden has said that he has begun repairing his fractured friendship with Nancy Pelosi, revealing in his new memoir that the two already reunited over lunch, RadarOnline.com has learned.

Their relationship deteriorated when the former House Speaker pushed him to abandon his 2024 reelection campaign.Joe Biden Shares Details of Private ReunionIn his upcoming memoir, Promise Me, America, Biden described meeting Pelosi for an Italian lunch after months of estrangement following his withdrawal from the presidential race.

"We had been through too much together to allow a rift to go un-mended," Biden wrote. "We talked about life and family and politics."

Biden said they quickly returned to the familiarity of their longtime friendship, although they deliberately avoided discussing the confrontation that had driven them apart.Biden's 2024 WithdrawalThe dispute began after Biden's June 27, 2024, presidential debate against Donald Trump, when his performance prompted Democratic leaders to question whether he should continue campaigning.

In his memoir, Biden accused Pelosi of working behind the scenes to persuade elected Democrats and convention delegates to withdraw their support. He also recalled that Pelosi challenged the information his advisers were providing about the election while making her own preference clear.

"She told me that I wasn't getting an honest assessment of where the race stood," Biden wrote.Biden's Confrontation With Chuck SchumerBiden also described a July 13, 2024, meeting with Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, who traveled to the president's home in Rehoboth Beach, Delaware, to urge him to withdraw.

"I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption... coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race," Biden penned.

He explained that he placed tremendous importance on loyalty and felt betrayed by political allies who had previously supported his presidency.The Day Biden WithdrewThe memoir also provides a detailed account of July 21, 2024, when Biden formally ended his reelection campaign after weeks of mounting pressure.

Biden wrote that he first notified campaign chair Jen O'Malley Dillon of his decision at 1:04 p.m. Seven minutes later, he called Vice President Kamala Harris, who repeatedly asked whether he was certain about withdrawing.

He then contacted Democratic lawmakers, governors and longtime political allies, including former President Bill Clinton at 3:14 p.m.

Biden ultimately endorsed Harris, who secured the Democratic nomination before losing the November election to Trump.
