news.title: Trump, Xi And Putin Summit Officially On The Books
news.text:
President Donald Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday for an unprecedented three-way summit involving the world’s leading nuclear powers.

China confirmed the Nov. 19 meeting in Shenzhen on Monday, following earlier announcements from Washington and Moscow, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry. The gathering will take place alongside the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, marking the first time the three leaders have met together in this format, the South China Morning Post reported.

The meeting will focus on international security and relations between the three nuclear powers, with Beijing describing the gathering as a historic diplomatic development, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry.

“The summit is of groundbreaking significance,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said during a Monday press briefing. (RELATED: Trump Could Bring Putin, Xi To Table As Nuclear Arms Race Looms)

The leaders intend to discuss safeguarding international peace and improving strategic stability between major powers, Mao added. Beijing argued that cooperation between Washington, Moscow and China could help address international security challenges, according to the Foreign Ministry.

However, the three governments have not publicly announced a comprehensive agenda, leaving questions about whether the summit will produce any substantive agreements.

Trump intends to make nuclear weapons reductions a central topic of discussion, according to Reuters, citing White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales.

“He will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” Wales said during a Friday briefing, according to Reuters.

The administration hopes the meeting will encourage China to participate in broader nuclear arms control negotiations, potentially establishing the foundation for a new agreement involving all three countries, Reuters reported, citing a senior administration official.

However, American officials have cautioned against expecting an immediate breakthrough.

“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official told Reuters.

China has repeatedly rejected American attempts to include Beijing in trilateral nuclear arms control negotiations, arguing that its nuclear capabilities remain substantially smaller than those maintained by Washington and Moscow.

“It is neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage,” Mao said during an Oct. 16 press briefing.

The three countries collectively maintain the overwhelming majority of the world’s nuclear weapons, although their individual stockpiles vary considerably, according to the Federation of American Scientists. Russia maintains an estimated 4,400 nuclear warheads in its military stockpile, compared with approximately 3,700 American warheads and 620 Chinese warheads, according to the organization’s 2026 estimates.

Those figures exclude retired weapons awaiting dismantlement. Including those weapons, Russia possesses approximately 5,420 warheads, while the United States maintains roughly 5,042, according to the Federation of American Scientists.

China’s arsenal remains considerably smaller than those of its rivals, but Beijing has continued expanding its nuclear capabilities while Washington and Moscow pursue modernization programs, according to the Federation of American Scientists.

The summit also follows the expiration of New START, the last remaining major nuclear arms control agreement between Washington and Moscow.

The treaty expired in February. It previously limited deployed strategic nuclear weapons and established verification procedures between the two countries, according to the State Department.

Trump rejected a Russian proposal to voluntarily maintain the treaty’s deployment limits for another year, instead advocating a replacement agreement, Reuters reported.

Beyond nuclear arms control, Trump intends to raise the ongoing American war against Iran during Thursday’s meeting, Reuters reported, citing a senior administration official.

The discussions could provide Washington another opportunity to engage Beijing and Moscow over the conflict, although neither government has publicly committed to participating in a new diplomatic initiative.

China has already dispatched diplomatic representatives to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia to discuss regional tensions and encourage negotiations, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry.

Beijing has called for de-escalation and a political settlement to the fighting, arguing that international cooperation is necessary to prevent renewed hostilities, according to the Foreign Ministry.

Notably, Trump is not expected to raise Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine during the three-way meeting, Reuters reported, citing an administration official.

Trump is also not expected to hold a separate bilateral meeting with Putin during his trip, although he plans to meet individually with Xi, Reuters reported, citing administration officials.

The unprecedented meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin would give Trump a direct opportunity to press Putin to end the Russo-Ukrainian War, fulfilling a central campaign promise that remains unrealized nearly two years after his return to the White House.

Trump repeatedly promised to resolve the conflict before taking office or within 24 hours of returning to the presidency. A review of his campaign statements identified at least 53 occasions when Trump made such pledges, CNN reported.

“Before I even arrive at the Oval Office, I will have the disastrous war between Russia and Ukraine settled,” Trump declared during a March 4, 2023, speech at the Conservative Political Action Conference, according to FactCheck.org. Trump added that resolving the conflict would take him “no longer than one day.”

“If I’m president, I will have that war settled in one day, 24 hours,” Trump said during a May 10, 2023, CNN town hall. Trump specifically proposed meeting Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to negotiate an agreement, arguing that both leaders had weaknesses he could exploit during negotiations.

“I will have that war settled between Putin and Zelenskyy as president-elect before I take office on January 20th,” Trump reiterated during his June 27, 2024, presidential debate against former President Joe Biden, according to the debate transcript.

Trump repeated that promise during his Sept. 10, 2024, debate against former Vice President Kamala Harris, arguing that personal relationships with both leaders would allow him to negotiate an agreement before his inauguration. “I will get it settled before I even become president,” Trump said, according to the debate transcript.

The planned meeting follows a Nov. 11 telephone conversation between Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi concerning bilateral relations and upcoming presidential engagements, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry.

Both governments expressed interest in maintaining stable relations and managing disagreements ahead of the summit, according to Beijing’s official readout.

Thursday’s gathering will coincide with APEC’s annual leaders’ meeting, scheduled for Nov. 18-19 in Shenzhen, according to the organization.

The 21-member economic forum is focused on international trade, technological development and regional economic cooperation, including artificial intelligence and supply chain resilience, according to APEC. (RELATED: US Army Practices Island Warfare As China’s Shadow Looms Large Over Pacific)

Despite the historic nature of the gathering, uncertainty remains over whether Beijing will accept American demands for nuclear negotiations or whether the summit will produce more than a preliminary diplomatic understanding.

Chinese officials have not committed to nuclear reductions, instead emphasizing the importance of maintaining communication and addressing broader international security challenges, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry.
news.summary: ‘The summit is of groundbreaking significance’

news.title: Republicans overwhelmed
news.text: Serious folks in the Grand Old Party are still trying to figure out why the party fared so badly in the November 3 mid-terms. So are the political strategists who are getting ready for the 2028 hopefuls, the signs for which have started to slowly emerge in both Republican and Democratic parties. Still, many are yet to get over the shocker: since the end of World War II, only three times has the House of Representatives and Senate flipped from one party to another in the same mid-terms: in 1946, 1994 and 2006. It happened for the fourth time in 2026. It was not just a question of Democrats getting hold of the House and the Senate. The sweep appears everywhere including at State houses and in Governor’s Mansions. The Democrats could control as many as 30 Governorships when the final results are declared. In a nutshell, the Republicans have taken a severe beating in places like Georgia, Texas, Ohio, South Carolina, North Carolina and New Hampshire. Overall tally The “Firsts” of a Black, Hispanic and Native American women getting elected as Governors of Georgia, Texas and New Mexico respectively were stunning indeed, but the overall tally in the House and Senate has left Republicans crestfallen: with about ten seats yet to be finalised in the House, Democrats have picked up 42 for a total of 256 as opposed to 169 for the GOP. Alaska is yet to called officially in the Senate but Democrats are up by eight members, currently posting a strength of 55. The pain for the GOP is not confined to numbers nationally or in the states. It is of a party that has been abandoned by the same group of folks who crossed over from Democrats in 2024. For instance, it is pointed out that voters under 30 were about evenly split between President Donald Trump and Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024; in the mid-terms 70 per cent of voters in this age category maintain they supported a Democratic candidate in their constituency. Like-wise if four out of 10 Hispanic voters backed President Trump in 2024, this time around six out of 10 said they had voted for a Democrat in the local House election. Analyses have shown that the Hispanics’ shift has been profound in the Congressional districts along the Texas-Mexico border, for example. Immigration enforcement and anger against the ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) are seen as a prominent reason for the switch. Black Americans or the African American community also moved away from the GOP in larger numbers — Black men especially, with Black women holding steady at earlier lower levels of support. Hispanics and Blacks were particularly incensed at re-districting that started in Texas but soon moved on a national scale with Democrats also playing the tit-for-tat game. Also, the crackdown on diversity initiatives by the Trump administration as also in trying to re-write history of race didn’t go down well with them. The voice of the Black people could not have resonated more than in Mississippi where the soon to be Senator Scott Colum beat the incumbent Republican by a razor thin margin, in a state where Black voters, at 37 per cent, are a larger population than any other state and has not sent a Democratic Senator since the time of segregation. As LaTosha Brown, the co-founder of Black Voters Matter said, “We can smell racism. We can see it … we can feel it, and we know how to respond to it. Our survival has been based on our ability to resist it and respond and navigate around it.” The real heartbreak for Republicans came from Evangelical Christians who voted overwhelmingly for GOP candidates, but a lower turnout cost the party. According to one estimate, some 82 per cent of Evangelicals supported Republicans but the national vote declined from 23 per cent to 17 per cent. Or as a former worship leader put it, “The Church stayed home!” The writer is a senior journalist who has reported from Washington DC on North America and United Nations

The United States has established Task Force Iron Gate to target weapons, sanctioned goods and illicit revenue moving through Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea—reinforcing the naval blockade rather than replacing it. The regime will sacrifice ordinary Iranians before abandoning the IRGC. It can print money, raise prices, seize revenue and strip civilian budgets to keep security forces loyal. But every rial redirected toward the IRGC deepens inflation, wage delays and public anger. Every unpaid soldier weakens the machinery responsible for protecting the regime and suppressing dissent. This does not prove the Islamic Republic is about to collapse. It shows that U.S. pressure is reaching beyond Iran’s economy and into the payroll of the regime’s survival apparatus. An authoritarian state can survive unpaid factory workers. It becomes far more vulnerable when it struggles to pay the men ordered to keep it in power.— The Iran Watcher (@TheIranWatcher) November 13, 2026

Here's one account from laid off law enforcement who says they're close to the tipping point where there's no fear or respect of police from Iranian civilians. 

The Islamic Republic’s law-enforcement forces are confronting collapsing morale and public contempt as their uniform becomes associated with repression, humiliation and mass killing. A video circulating from a recently discharged police conscript gives voice to a broader crisis inside the security apparatus. He says the era of automatically respecting military and law-enforcement personnel is over. Many Iranians now view those in uniform as “mercenaries,” “repressors” and “murderers” because they participated in the January 2026 massacre—or remained silent while it happened. Estimates place the death toll at more than 45,000. The United Nations later concluded that the regime’s widespread killings, imprisonment, torture and other abuses amounted to "crimes against humanity." But public hatred was not created by the massacre alone. These are also the forces that patrol streets, harass women, arrest them over hijab compliance and subject ordinary Iranians to daily intimidation and humiliation. The uniform no longer represents public safety. For many Iranians, it represents the officer checking a woman’s clothing, the van taking her away and the armed personnel firing on protesters. This anger extends beyond senior commanders or ideological members of the IRGC and Basij. It increasingly follows police officers, regular military personnel and young men completing compulsory service. Not everyone wearing the uniform supports the Islamic Republic. Milad Moazami Goodarzi reportedly came from the military ranks but stood with the people and was killed during the January uprising. Others may privately oppose the regime while remaining trapped inside its institutions. But the regime deliberately erased that distinction by using every security branch - including compulsory-service conscripts - to control the population. When society despises the uniform, personnel lose more than public respect. Their families face shame, their communities distrust them and their own belief in the institution begins to weaken. That directly damages morale, cohesion, recruitment and obedience across the security apparatus. The Islamic Republic can force young Iranians to serve, order them into the streets and place weapons in their hands. It cannot force the Iranian people to respect them—or prevent its own forces from feeling the shame attached to the uniform they wear. https://t.co/tmJjiqqEYs— The Iran Watcher (@TheIranWatcher) November 13, 2026

Gasoline remains a scarcity the regime cannot provide. They've never had the refining capacity internally to handle the daily demand, and the regime has compounded the problem for decades by subsidizing gas, conditioning the population to pay a price per liter well below market value. Now that they can no longer import gasoline to meet the demand, and no longer has the cash reserves to keep the subsidy going, the lines Iranians wait in only get longer as each day exacerbates the supply problem. 

🚨 IRAN: Long Queues and Fuel Protests - Next Uprising on the Way? Long gas queues and protests are escalating across the country on the Nov. 2019 uprising anniversary, when fuel hikes sparked a nationwide revolt that pushed the regime to the brink. https://t.co/1QOR2Q0j2V— Ehsan Eghbal Eslami (@Ehsaneghbale) November 14, 2026

A video sent to Iran International shows a long line of vehicles waiting for fuel at a gas station in Sadra, a city northwest of Shiraz in southern Iran's Fars province. https://t.co/61mi5HJpas— Iran International English (@IranIntl_En) November 14, 2026

A third of Trump's base protested high gas prices by sitting on their hands, or worse, casting votes for a political party that historically views high gas prices as a feature, not a bug. Not one of them had to wait in a line like this just to buy it. How do Iranians react to their gasoline reality? 

Fuel unrest has erupted in Iran as furious drivers begin blocking highways over gasoline shortages. On Friday night, residents reportedly parked their cars and blocked Rajaei Highway outside the Aftab Derakhshan gas station in Bandar Abbas after stations ran short of fuel. Videos show crowds gathering and traffic brought to a halt. The unrest remains localized for now, but gasoline has triggered nationwide upheaval before. In November 2019, a sudden fuel-price increase ignited protests across Iran within days. The Islamic Republic shut down the internet and opened fire on demonstrators. Amnesty International documented at least 304 deaths, while Reuters reported that approximately 1,500 people were killed. That history explains why the regime is tightening access gradually instead of announcing one dramatic nationwide increase. Emergency station cards are being withdrawn across multiple provinces, forcing drivers to depend on personal fuel cards. After the subsidized quotas are exhausted, additional gasoline costs 10,000 tomans per litre. The regime calls this “demand management” and an effort to combat smuggling. In practice, it is transferring the cost of fuel shortages and financial collapse onto ordinary Iranians. The contradiction is explosive: Iran possesses some of the world’s largest oil reserves, yet people in Hormozgan—a province containing major refineries—are struggling to obtain gasoline. Fuel shortages affect nearly everyone. They prevent people from reaching work, operating taxis, transporting goods and earning a living. Local anger can therefore spread far faster than protests confined to one profession or social group. The Bandar Abbas blockade does not yet constitute a national uprising. But the Islamic Republic knows that Iran’s largest protest waves have often begun with an economic grievance before rapidly becoming a political revolt against the entire system. The first highway has been blocked. In Iran, history shows how quickly a gasoline crisis can become something much larger. https://t.co/TGN7xGESh5— The Iran Watcher (@TheIranWatcher) November 13, 2026

Cab drivers began to get into the act. 

Taxi drivers have joined Iran’s growing strike wave as the fuel and cost-of-living crisis spreads across the country. Taxi drivers in Ardabil stopped working on November 14, parking rows of yellow taxis beneath an overpass in protest over rising gasoline prices, low fares and collapsing living standards. The strike follows fuel-related unrest in Bandar Abbas, where angry drivers blocked Rajaei Highway after gas stations ran short of gasoline. Bus and minibus drivers in Yazd have also stopped working over unpaid revenue and rising vehicle costs. Snapp drivers, truckers, waste workers and factory employees have held strikes or demonstrations in several other cities. The immediate trigger is gasoline, but the crisis is much larger. The Islamic Republic has increased above-quota fuel prices, restricted access to emergency station cards and forced drivers to rely on personal allocations that often do not cover their work. Taxi drivers are being crushed between higher fuel, maintenance and replacement-part costs and fares that passengers can barely afford. Working longer no longer guarantees that they can support their families. This is politically dangerous because economic strikes have repeatedly become something much larger in Iran. In late 2025, strikes and demonstrations triggered by economic collapse expanded into the nationwide anti-regime uprising of January 2026. What began with demands over wages, prices and survival became a direct challenge to the Islamic Republic. The same danger exists now. Taxi and transport strikes are particularly disruptive because they connect fuel shortages to everyday life. They affect workers, passengers, businesses, food distribution and movement between cities. The Ardabil strike remains local, and it is too early to call it the beginning of another national uprising. But the Islamic Republic is again confronting the same combustible combination: fuel shortages, unaffordable prices, unpaid wages, collapsing purchasing power and workers who no longer believe the system can provide them with a future. Taxi drivers have now joined the unrest. Iran’s recent history shows how quickly a livelihood protest can become a revolt against the entire regime. https://t.co/KBInbv6bEb— The Iran Watcher (@TheIranWatcher) November 14, 2026

High-profile members of the regime are sparring with each other publicly. 

Infighting inside the Islamic Republic is breaking into public view as Ghalibaf fights to reclaim a negotiation file increasingly seized by Rezaei. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf just publicly insisted that he remains in charge of negotiations with the United States, declaring: “I take responsibility as its chief” and “leading the negotiations and taking follow-up measures rests with me.” But Ghalibaf has been publicly sidelined as Mohsen Rezaei increasingly takes control of the file, dictates the regime’s conditions and emerges as its authoritative voice. Rezaei recently travelled to Russia to deliver a personal message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to Vladimir Putin. He discussed the war, regional security and the Islamic Republic’s seven conditions for negotiations. He then declared that the regime would neither reopen the Strait of Hormuz nor negotiate until the United States implemented those demands. JD Vance’s reported letter proposing a direct meeting was also sent to Rezaei—not Ghalibaf. That fuelled speculation that control of the file had shifted from Ghalibaf’s formal negotiating team to the Supreme National Security Council and its new secretary. Ghalibaf’s Al Jazeera interview was therefore not only directed at the United States. It was also a message inside the Islamic Republic that he refuses to accept his relegation while Rezaei assumes the more powerful diplomatic and security role. Ghalibaf insisted that the negotiating team had not changed, that the United States had failed to provide an official response and that the regime’s seven conditions must be implemented before Hormuz reopens or negotiations resume. But Ghalibaf is fighting to control a diplomatic process that the United States may no longer want. President Trump has now declared: “We don’t need a deal with Iran.” That statement does more than reject the Islamic Republic’s conditions. It undercuts the entire negotiation track and further diminishes Ghalibaf’s importance. Ghalibaf is asserting his authority as chief negotiator at the same moment Trump is saying there is no need to negotiate. Rezaei’s security-first approach therefore carries greater weight inside the regime, while Ghalibaf risks retaining a title attached to a process that has lost its American counterpart. Both men are longtime IRGC figures deeply embedded within the Islamic Republic. Rezaei commanded the IRGC from 1981 to 1997 and represents its older, more rigid military-security establishment. Ghalibaf also rose through the IRGC but became a more politically agile operator through his roles as police chief, mayor and parliamentary speaker. Neither is a moderate or an opponent of the regime. The difference is one of style, institutional power and control. Ghalibaf presents the regime’s demands as the basis for a political negotiation. Rezaei presents the same demands as conditions for American capitulation and dismisses reports of meaningful talks as “imaginary.” The Islamic Republic officially denies that Ghalibaf has been sidelined. But officials do not repeatedly insist that a negotiator remains in charge unless serious questions about his authority have emerged. This is not yet an open struggle for control of the entire regime, and there is no evidence that either man faces an imminent purge. But the competition is real and increasingly visible. Ghalibaf retains the formal title of chief negotiator. Rezaei increasingly appears to possess the Supreme Leader’s confidence, the authority of the security apparatus and the power to determine what negotiations can—and cannot—deliver. Trump’s rejection of a deal makes the contradiction even sharper. Ghalibaf is fighting to control negotiations that may no longer exist, while Rezaei is consolidating control over the regime’s response to their failure. The struggle is therefore no longer only over who negotiates with the United States. It is over who speaks for the Islamic Republic when the United States refuses to negotiate at all.— The Iran Watcher (@TheIranWatcher) November 12, 2026

Secretary Bessent compared the stress fractures Iran is facing to those that caused the Soviet Union to crumble. 

BREAKING: US SEC. BESSENT ON IRAN: “March of 2026 to March of 2027, The rial will collapse 25% in one year. To put that in perspective, the Russian economy went down 22% over three years when the Soviet Union collapsed.” https://t.co/Zc9ZHXHDN6— Sulaiman Ahmed (@ShaykhSulaiman) November 15, 2026

While the regime wriggles around in the noose, American forces are as numerous in the region as they have been since the war began. 

U.S. Aircraft in theater: 300+— Open Source Intel (@Osint613) November 15, 2026

All seems like it's going according to plan, right? Not entirely. In Yemen, the hot war zone between the Houthis, the last remaining Iranian terror proxy, and the coalition of Yemeni government forces, loyal tribal brigades, Saudi air assets and Pakistani and Turk defensive forces, has taken an alarming turn in the last 24 hours. The Bab al-Mandeb Strait has fallen...again.

Not great, Bab.For the last six weeks, Yemen government forces, with Saudi air support, chased out and largely held former Houthi strongholds along the coast, and the fighting was concentrated largely in the mountainous region of Taiz. The fighting there continues -- a lot of anti-tank shelling, but a lot more on both sides via drone strikes. But yesterday, the Yemen forces headquartered in Aden to the south confirmed they are pulling back to defensible lines to protect the back-up capital city. Not a good development at all. 

Pro-govt Southern Armed Forces announced a redeployment of their troops from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area west of #Taiz, citing the need to reinforce security in Aden and neighbouring provinces amid recent military developments and Houthi threats. "In light of recent developments on the battlefronts, military buildups and threats targeting the temporary capital, Aden, and neighbouring provinces, as well as the responsibilities and operational and security priorities imposed by the current phase, the Southern Armed Forces announce that they are redeploying their forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area in western Taiz province. The move is part of efforts to reorganise their deployment and strengthen their presence in areas and sectors required by the demands of the current phase." The forces said the move would also support efforts to break the Houthi siege on Taiz and end the suffering of its residents, reaffirming that their military campaign against the Iran-backed Houthis would continue. #Yemen— Ali Al-Sakani | علي السكني (@Alsakaniali) November 15, 2026

Last week, there was a pretty significant air assault on the Houthi stronghold up north in Sana'a. This week, the Houthis successfully pushed back the other direction. And as of last night, reports surfaced of bombing in Aden. 

Two explosions rocked #Aden city moments ago.
#Yemen— Ali Al-Sakani | علي السكني (@Alsakaniali) November 15, 2026

This has been a see-saw affair for the last few weeks. Both sides are losing a lot of people and tons of drones. Saudi Arabia should have air superiority over anything the Houthis can fly, but the Houthis still have a bunch of Iranian-made missiles, and they've been using them as of late. My friend and podcast partner from the Reagan Institute, former Missouri Senator Jim Talent, has said for the past few weeks that the Houthis are going to have to be addressed by the U.S., and it was almost a certainty that the President would eventually authorize a tipping of the scales there to give the Arab nations a little edge over the terror proxy. Yesterday's gains by the Houthis, if held, are untenable in the long run. Hormuz is still the primary artery for oil leaving the Gulf region, but a virulent Houthi terror group choking off the secondary chokepoint and threatening the Saudi East-West pipeline once again, and perhaps even the Suez Canal, cannot be allowed to fester. We have three carrier groups and 300 aircraft in the region, and that's not including our long-range bombers we can load up from here. That's more than enough firepower to mow the lawn in Sana'a as well keeping weeds from popping up in Hormuz. Overall, as we begin to think about the holidays beginning next week, the Iran problem does seem to be working itself out, albeit agonizingly slowly. Could that change? Sure, especially if the Houthis do establish the upper hand and throw a monkey wrench into the oil market that is well on its way to recovery. Let's hope that Yemen gets a little personalized attention fairly soon. It will give me a little more to be thankful for a week from Thursday.

news.title: Who will carry MAGA’s torch in 2028 — and who will challenge? Stu Burguiere and Dave Landau weigh the contenders
news.text:
The 2028 presidential race is still two years away, but the potential contenders are already jockeying for position.

Democrats are weighing possible campaigns by Kamala Harris and Gavin Newsom, while Republicans are beginning to consider who could carry the MAGA movement beyond Donald Trump.

On “Stu Does America,” BlazeTV host Stu Burguiere and co-host Dave Landau size up the early field, including Pete Buttigieg, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, JD Vance, Marco Rubio, Ron DeSantis, and Ted Cruz.

But not everyone on the list impresses Stu. When the conversation turns to Buttigieg, Stu questions whether the former transportation secretary has what it takes to win the nomination.

 - YouTube 

“I guess nothing, is what I would say about him. He doesn’t have it. I think he’s unemployed currently,” Stu says.

“Cyclist?” Dave asks, joking. “I mean, he gets dropped off in an SUV mere blocks away, but still a cyclist, environmental-friendly cyclist.”

“One of my favorite stories of the entire Biden administration: when he, as transportation secretary, allegedly rode his bike, or took his bike in the back of an SUV until he got close so then it could look like he was riding his bike to work,” Stu recalls.

“So pathetic,” he adds.

Of the stronger candidates, Stu says Gavin Newsom appears to be positioning himself for a presidential run. He points to a recent interview Newsom did with Jake Tapper while the pair were fly-fishing.

During the interview, Newsom suggested he wouldn't run if Kamala Harris entered the race.

“That one actually made me think he was more likely to run, and it made me think that Kamala Harris was less likely to run,” Stu says.

“At no point did I think that Gavin Newsom was not going to run,” he adds.

As for Republicans, JD Vance would appear to be the top contender.

“Of course, it would make sense. JD Vance would be the guy,” Stu says.

“Why wouldn’t [Trump] endorse Vance? He already picked him as the guy who’s one breath away from the presidency,” he adds.

Stu also sees Secretary of State Marco Rubio as a potential contender.

“Marco Rubio, I think, would probably do a good job as well. Rubio has been seen as very competent in this administration. The media kind of hates everybody in this administration, but sort of seems to have a soft spot for Marco Rubio.”

“Now, the second he runs for president, obviously that will go away. But, you know, Rubio has said if Vance runs, he probably won’t,” he adds.

news.title: In Conversation With Peggy Flanagan, The First Native Woman Elected To The Senate
news.text:
WASHINGTON – More than 2,000 people have served as U.S. senators since the country’s founding. Just 65 have been women.

None has been a Native American woman.

Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) is about to change that. After a resounding midterm victory, Flanagan, an Ojibwe citizen of the White Earth Nation, is headed to Washington, D.C., as a historic first and one of eight new Democrats who won on Nov. 3 and helped flip Senate control to their party. If Mary Peltola wins her race in Alaska, she’ll be the Senate’s ninth new Democrat and its second Indigenous woman.

Flanagan’s path to the Senate meant overcoming a bitter primary race against Democratic Rep. Angie Craig and taking on conservative media personality Michele Tafoya in November. It also involved navigating the violence and terror of Operation Metro Surge, the Trump administration’s siege on immigrants in the state. This was easily the single-most animating issue of Minnesota’s election cycle, and one that Flanagan, a progressive who has served as her state’s lieutenant governor for the last eight years, loudly condemned.

Toward the end of Flanagan’s campaign, some political observers suggested she was underperforming, as she led in public polling by just a few percentage points in a blue state, at a time when President Donald Trump’s poor approval ratings were hurting the GOP nationally. Flanagan’s team shrugged it off and stood by their internal polling, which showed her in a stronger position. 

On Election Day, she defeated Tafoya by more than 10 percentage points – more than double the margin that former Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris won the state in 2024.

HuffPost recently caught up with Flanagan to talk about her historic win, how she feels people underestimated her Senate bid “every step of the way,” her plan to “avenge Minnesota” for ICE’s assault on residents, and why she thinks it’s time for Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to step aside and let someone new guide the party forward.

Here’s a transcript of our interview, lightly edited for brevity.

HuffPost: Congratulations on your Senate victory. What does the historic aspect of your win mean to you personally?

Peggy Flanagan: It has been deeply humbling, and when I think about it too long, like right now, I become pretty emotional. One of the things we did for Senate orientation is we went to the National Archives. We were there in the gigantic room where the Declaration of Independence is held and, you know, it’s a document that contains the phrase “merciless Indian savages.”

We are in the room where there is the first treaty that the Iroquois Confederacy signed, the treaty between the United States and the Six Nations. It was the first one following the Revolutionary War. That struck me. In the back of the room, there’s the Emancipation Proclamation. I stood there with my husband for a minute, and I was like, look at this room. The first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate is here. The first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate is in this room. The second Black woman from the state of Illinois is in this room. 

Only in America is that possible. So, I’ve been pretty up in my feels.

But it really is that I want young Native women and girls to see, you know, “If Auntie Peggy can do it, I can do it too.” Just knowing they will get here much faster than I did, and part of my job is being someone who has broken a ceiling. The cuts and bruises and shrapnel and scars, I’ll take that. Because then they don’t have to go through it. And that’s the work.

HP: Are you ready to duke it out with Mary Peltola for the title of first Indigenous woman in the Senate?

PF: She’ll be the first Alaska Native woman. I’ll be the first Native American woman. We’ll see whose results get certified first… The beautiful thing right now that there’s two of us is we’re a parity. It’s about time. It’s exciting.

HP: You won your race by more than 10 points. There were some rumblings toward the end of the campaign that you might be in trouble, that the margins were looking smaller than they should. Do you feel that people were underestimating you in your campaign?

HP: Alrighty then!

PF: Listen, we were underestimated every step of the way. In the primary and in the general, Minnesotans proved people wrong. I think so many folks doubted my ability to win on a populist, progressive message in the general election. And we won, as you said, by over 10 points.

We were able to do, I think it was over 360 events and 125 communities that I did personally. That’s including places that hadn’t seen a statewide candidate in over a decade. The vision our campaign really set out to deliver was a vision of helping Minnesotans afford the lives they want to live, and that resonated across the state. We also organized the heck out of this campaign. The party knocked on almost 3 million doors. We get what we organized for, and that’s really what a people-powered campaign that refused corporate PAC money looks like.

HP: You think it’s time for Chuck Schumer to step aside as Senate Democratic leader, and you’re backing Chris Van Hollen for the job. What do you say to those who say Schumer just earned his leadership job because of his role in Democrats’ big wins in the midterms?

PF: I’ve been in communication with Chuck Schumer over the last several weeks and months, and I’m tremendously grateful for his leadership and what he’s done for years and years. But I do think it’s time for new leadership. People voted for change, and we are at a point of a new movement in this country. We just elected a new generation of leaders, many of whom refused corporate PAC money. We’re beholden only to the people who elected us and who are ready to fight for bold change. I think it’s time.

And when Donald Trump makes [anti-immigrant extremist] Stephen Miller his chief of staff, and when [Minnesota Republican Rep.] Tom Emmer basically threatens his colleagues, we need people who are ready to be fighters. We’re not gonna, you know, nice-y nice our way through this moment. And Minnesotans have seen what this administration is capable of. We need leaders who are ready to push back and throw down.

HP: And that’s not Chuck Schumer.

PF: I don’t think it is.

I would say this: When there is the laundry list of things that Democrats need to do, [which is] what we hear from leadership, we also need to hear that we are going to take on ICE. The fact that there have been no consequences, no accountability, even no sharing of evidence, no investigation of the killing of Alex Pretti and Renee Good? That needs to be on the tip of your tongue, that you are interested in leading in this moment.

We have seen the worst of this administration up close. We need to make sure that our leaders understand what their assignment is, too.

HP: What are your top priorities once you’re sworn in January?

PF: I am very clear that rolling back these cuts to Medicaid and SNAP are at the top of the list. The impact on the most vulnerable people in the state and the impact on rural hospitals and clinics is so clear. When I talk to people who are part of food shelves across the state who are saying the need is so high, higher than we’ve ever seen, and the resources so low, we’ve got to do better and help to repair some of the damage this president has done.

I’ve talked about Medicare for All, and that’s absolutely something we need to fight for. I’m eager we’re on the way to ban prior authorization. Farmers should be able to fix their own damn equipment, that’s something I want to lead on as well. Raising the minimum wage. Ending this war. That’s on the list.

And of course, holding this administration accountable for the damage they’ve done across the board, but specifically, I have said that I want to avenge Minnesota. What that means is accountability for the damage that was done, the chaos and the terror that’s been inflicted on Minnesota through Operation Metro Surge.

HP: Did you see that Aliya Rahman, the Minneapolis woman whose image went viral in January when ICE agents violently dragged her out of her car, just sued the U.S. government over that?

PF: I’m grateful she has the courage to fight for justice knowing that it’s not just about her, but about all the people who have been impacted by the ICE thugs in our streets.

HP: Did you see that ICE has been quietly deleting its past tweets critical of Rahman?

PF: See? Like, this is the thing. They know. They know. And they are telling on themselves every day.

HP: Last thing. You’re part of this new band of progressives joining the Senate. Juliana Stratton of Illinois. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan. Troy Jackson of Maine. Do you feel like collectively you are bringing something to the Senate that its current crop of Democratic senators does not have?

PF: We are fresh off the campaign, coming in with the largest class of Democrats that’s been elected in decades, so I think we’ve got a lot of energy. Many of us understood the assignment of not taking corporate PAC money and are beholden only to the people who sent us to Washington, D.C. I’m excited about what that means and what that looks like for this class, but also for the country.

HP: Anything else you think people should know about you?

PF: You know, I’m a mom. I hope I’m a cool mom. I like big earrings. That’s not a secret. I hope to introduce ribbon skirts into the United States Senate. I’m gonna dress like myself.

Maybe that’s the biggest thing for folks to know. I’m just a normal person. For this class, there’s so many of us who, like, this will be our job, and our salary, and we are looking for places to live, and just trying to figure it all out. I think that’s good for the Senate, and frankly, I think it’s good for democracy.

news.title: Biden library nears site decision as fundraising lags
news.text: The foundation building Joe Biden's presidential library is nearing a decision on a site in Delaware, as it tries to gain fundraising momentum after bringing in less than $1.5 million in 2025, according to sources familiar with the planning and a copy of its most recent tax filing obtained by CBS News.The Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation spent about $2.1 million last year, mostly on staff, consultants and legal fees, running a deficit of around $600,000, according to the filing. The document, which covers the foundation's first full calendar year and does not cover 2026 activity, was submitted to the IRS and has not been made public.Board members met last week to discuss the library, and an announcement on the site is expected in the next couple of months, the sources said. In 2026, the foundation stepped up its fundraising, securing several multimillion-dollar donations, including two $5 million gifts, one of the sources said. They spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal planning and fundraising.Last week, the Biden library foundation added five new board members, an official for the foundation said. They include Elizabeth Frawley Bagley, Biden's former ambassador to Brazil and a longtime Democratic fundraiser; Bijan Sabet, a venture capitalist who served as his ambassador to the Czech Republic; event planner Bryan Rafanelli; Wilmington nonprofit leader Logan Herring; and Annie Tomasini, a former White House deputy chief of staff who will remain the group's co-executive director.The official for the foundation declined to share an estimate of the expected cost of the library, but said the group expects to do so when it announces its site. It finished 2025 with about $3.4 million in net assets, the filing shows.The fundraising push is an early test of Democratic donors' appetite for a project meant to further shape the legacy of Biden's presidency and a political career that spanned more than half a century. Biden is out with a memoir, "Promise Me, America," to be published on Tuesday. He announced that he would be scaling back the book tour amid his cancer treatment.Modern presidential centers cost hundreds of millions of dollars and rely on large checks from individual and corporate donors. The foundation is now courting donors after a midterm cycle that drew heavily from ultra-wealthy Democrats.The nonprofit's fundraising pace stands in stark contrast to President Trump's library foundation, which has already raised tens of millions of dollars, including from media and tech companies that settled lawsuits with him. That includes large donations from Meta, Elon Musk's X, and Paramount, which paid $16 million over the editing of a "60 Minutes" interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. (Paramount reached the settlement before its merger with Skydance Media. The combined company, Skydance, is CBS News' parent company.)The official for the Biden library foundation said it wasn't actively fundraising in 2025, describing it as a "building and infrastructure year." The money for this came from Biden's presidential inaugural committee, his transition fund and two individual donors whom the foundation official declined to name also made unsolicited donations. The filing shows the foundation paid about $250,000 last year to consultants for "fundraising counsel." This was meant to lay the groundwork for its fundraising push in 2026, including a feasibility study on its donor base and advice on how to structure its fundraising team, the official for the foundation said.Biden, who served one term, waited until the final weeks of his presidency to set up a library foundation, while several predecessors began theirs during their second terms. The foundation was incorporated in December 2024 and listed $4 million in contributions, which the foundation official described as seed money, on its first tax filing. By comparison, former President Barack Obama's foundation was formed in early 2014, nearly three years before he left office, and raised $5.4 million that year, even as Obama capped donations at $1 million and did not solicit publicly. It raised a staggering $232 million in 2017, his first year after leaving the White House. Former President George W. Bush's foundation raised $27.5 million from 2006 to 2008, while he was still in office, and $152 million in 2009.The Biden library foundation did not receive tax-exempt status from the IRS until March 2025, about two months after Biden left office. It announced its board in September of that year and said the library would be in his home state of Delaware.Some of Biden's close allies have privately been frustrated with Democratic donors for not proactively reaching out to support his library, according to a source familiar with the matter. That frustration has grown amid reports of the haul by President Trump's library, which includes $50 million from SoftBank, the Japanese investment giant.Biden has "never been a good fundraiser, even when he was in the Senate," the source said. Former first lady Jill Biden is expected to help out on fundraising while also caring for Biden as he gets treated for prostate cancer that has metastasized to his bones, they added.An official for the Biden library foundation said it is "not comparing" itself to Mr. Trump's library. "We're running very different types of organizations," the official said. Mr. Trump's library is facing scrutiny from Democrats, who take control of Congress in January and have vowed to investigate its finances. Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who has said donors "will have to answer to a new majority in Congress," opened an inquiry over the summer into SoftBank's donation — which came two months before the Trump administration announced a federal land lease for a SoftBank data center in Ohio. The Energy Department has said the lease was signed in February and that a local group first proposed the project in October 2024. SoftBank referred CBS News to its July statement confirming the donation, which said the company "is proud of its support for institutions dedicated to preserving American history while continuing its commitment to investing in America's future."The Trump library foundation is also fundraising through a donation platform run by PublicSquare — a company whose board includes Donald Trump Jr., CBS News reported. The library foundation's trustees include Mr. Trump's son Eric and son-in-law Michael Boulos, corporate records filed in Florida show.An official for the Biden library foundation said its staff has worked to ensure there are "no conflict issues," noting that no members of the Biden family, including the former president and Jill Biden, sit on its board. The board is chaired by Rufus Gifford, a prolific Democratic fundraiser and former ambassador to Denmark under Obama. The board also includes former Secretary of State Antony Blinken and Biden adviser Steve Ricchetti, both of whom worked with Biden over a long stretch of his public life.The tax filing shows that the Biden library foundation paid over $221,000 each in compensation to its co-executive directors, Anthony Bernal, a longtime senior adviser to Jill Biden, and Annie Tomasini, a former White House deputy chief of staff. Their combined pay made up roughly a fifth of the foundation's spending last year.
news.summary: After a quiet 2025, Biden's presidential library foundation landed two $5 million gifts, but some allies are said to be frustrated donors haven't come calling.

news.title: Voter turnout dropped in Chicago's GOP strongholds, increased in areas affected by Operation Midway Blitz
news.text:
Traditional Republican strongholds in Chicago saw a decrease in voter turnout in the Nov. 3 election, while areas affected by Operation Midway Blitz saw a bump.

WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times examined the 90 precincts President Donald Trump won in 2024, which represent traditionally conservative areas of the city. Voter turnout in those precincts was down an average of 6.26 percentage points in the November election compared to 2022.

And traditionally Democratic precincts that voted for Kamala Harris saw an increase in voter turnout by an average of 3.23 percentage points.

The analysis is based on election results posted by the Chicago Board of Election Commissioners as of Friday afternoon.

At the same time, data shows voter turnout was up in neighborhoods affected by Operation Midway Blitz, including in Little Village, Pilsen, Humboldt Park and the South Shore neighborhood. During the height of the immigration enforcement, 3,841 people were detained. Only 15% of those detained had a criminal conviction.

In the South Shore raid on Sept. 30, 2025, allegedly acting on a tip from building management, federal agents rappelled down from helicopters, ransacked the building and zip-tied residents, many of them U.S. citizens. Government officials said they were going after members of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua, but no criminal charges have been filed against anyone arrested that night.

In the 7th Ward, where federal agents raided the South Shore building, voter turnout was up 5.3 percentage points.

In Little Village and surrounding neighborhoods, home to the 22nd Ward, all precincts saw an increase in voter turnout except for the precinct that is home to the Cook County Jail, which saw a drop of 6.5 percentage points compared to the 2022 midterms. Trump won that precinct in 2024. All precincts in Pilsen also saw increases in voter turnout.

All precincts in the 41st Ward on the Far Northwest Side also saw drops in voter turnout. The ward was the only in which Trump won more than half the votes in the November 2024 election.

Nearly all precincts in the 19th Ward, home to Beverly and Mount Greenwood, saw a double digit drop in voter turnout in the November election. The neighborhoods, home to police officers, firefighters and union workers, have historically shown support for GOP candidates.

Blue gains across Illinois

In Chicago, Trump jumped to 22.01% of the city vote in 2024, up from 12.41% of the city vote in 2016. In Illinois, Trump’s statewide vote grew to 45.3% in 2024, up from 38.76% in 2016, according to returns.

But the November election painted a picture of national dissatisfaction over Trump administration policies, including the war in Iran, which has directly impacted gas prices, as well as aggressive immigration efforts and general affordability issues affecting Americans.

With Democratic blowouts in favor of Gov. JB Pritzker, Attorney General Kwame Raoul, Comptroller-elect Margaret Croke and all other statewide officeholders, Illinois Republicans are finding themselves in dire straits.

Democrats even made inroads in territory long considered solid Republican ground, with Ricky Rivard unseating four-term GOP St. Charles state Rep. Dan Ugaste.

Rockford state Sen. Dave Syverson — the longest-serving member of the chamber, in office since 1993 — narrowly won against Democratic challenger Sarah Mertens, 50.8% to 49.2%.

Pritzker won his third term by his widest margin yet — 60.6% to Darren Bailey’s 36%. The Democratic governor also picked up red counties like Winnebago, McHenry, Sangamon and Jackson counties.

Operation Midway Blitz a motivating factor

Growing up in Little Village, Brenda Anaya said she grew accustomed to seeing the neighborhood bustling with people. But that changed when the Trump administration launched Operation Midway Blitz last fall.

As federal agents began filling the streets in search of undocumented immigrants, Anaya said residents grew fearful and stopped leaving their homes.

“A lot of people were scared,” said Anaya, 27. “It was a hard time for everyone living here.”

Anaya voted for Democrats in the midterm election and was confident they would win in Illinois. However, she was surprised to see Democratic victories extend beyond the state and across the country.

After Democrats gained control of both the U.S. Senate and U.S. House of Representatives during the midterm elections, Anaya said she’s beginning to hope things will return to normal.

“When [elected officials] come into office, I hope they do what they can to stop ICE,” she said.

Anaya hopes immigration enforcement will stop not only in Chicago but across the country.

“People should feel safe,” she said.

news.title: The chain-reaction era: Constant shock and awe
news.text:
Politics, AI, media and business are now one wired system: A jolt in one sets off the other three, instantly.

We call this post-processable velocity: Change is moving faster than any person, company, market or government can absorb.People's fears about AI are now mushrooming into jitteriness about civilization's connective tissue. An AP story on Sunday asked: "Could everything be broken?"Images of empty European supermarket refrigerators, cleared of spoiled food after a spate of mysterious cyberattacks, added to the sense that our connections are crumbling, with the simplest conveniences in danger.

What makes all this so disorienting for all of us is how interconnected politics, AI, business and media have become. The Nvidia spy scandal is a vivid example:

Media, last weekend: The New York Times reports that Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned President Trump that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang was tied to a suspected Chinese spy. Social media erupts. Business, Monday: Nvidia stock falls more than 4% at the open and keeps sliding. Fears of economy-wide AI fallout follow.Politics, all week: Trump's top team gets dragged into a "what did they know and when" frenzy. Democrats demand hearings.Policy, now: Lawmakers are scrambling to untangle the web of spies, lies and AI, and are racing to tighten China's access to Nvidia chips that gave Huang the power he's now surrendered.Tech, going forward: AI companies are rethinking their reliance on Nvidia chips and exploring financing options beyond Nvidia.

⏱️ Huang's resignation was announced just 14 days after last month's New York Times blockbuster exclusive that he was believed to be the target of a Chinese plot, and four days after he admitted an affair. 

One revelation, two weeks, and the most important CEO in AI is gone.

Three forces make this permanent:

🔄 1. Politics swings wildly. This was the seventh straight election in which the White House, Senate or House changed hands. And this time, in truly unthinkable and historic ways.

There were a number of "split districts" in 2024 that went for Kamala Harris for president and a Republican for the House. This year, every single one swung to electing a Democrat. We can't find any precedent for this.It's possible we've hit a post-ideological age where people feel very little affiliation to party tribes. How do you explain young men shifting almost 40 points from Republicans to Democrats in two years?

🤖 2. AI concentrates everything. A handful of companies are making historic bets on superhuman intelligence, and propping up the economy while they do it.

That puts enormous power and risk in very few hands. One man's affair shook the whole market.Nvidia makes the vital ingredient of AI, and helps finance nearly every big player buying it.But it's not just Nvidia. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft or Amazon can rattle the market with one announcement too.

⛓️‍💥 3. Everything is fragile when everything is interconnected. Friday's flight shutdown had nothing to do with AI, spies or elections, but it still shook us all.

It appears a contractor was swapping copper wire for fiber. Routers overloaded. Departures stopped nationwide for more than four hours.A total of 18,000+ U.S. flights were canceled over the past three days. Officials said little for hours. Rumors, speculation and gallows humor filled the void. "The aliens have landed," the novelist Stephen King tweeted. "That's the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don't want to start a worldwide panic."

The bottom line: The shocks will change. The speed won't.

news.title: Inside Jill Biden's fiercely guarded East Wing: Ugly blame game over 'catatonic' Joe... how the first lady would do anything to make the president 'look good'... and the 'work husband' who would 'crawl into a coffin with her'
news.text:
It was August 2021, and the disastrous fall of Kabul was underway, with the Taliban marching on the Afghan capital after President Joe Biden's chaotic withdrawal of US troops.

Everyone was mobilizing to try and help Afghans who had worked with the US military to escape, and former US first ladies were leaping into action. They had historically supported female empowerment in the country, aware that standing up for the rights of Afghan women was a cause that few could quibble with.

But even as rumors swirled that 'kills lists' of female Afghan activists were circulating, one emergency call at the White House allegedly had a different priority: how to shield First Lady Jill Biden from any political fallout.

'Hillary Clinton and Laura Bush mobilized their usual networks to mount independent missions to evacuate Afghan women,' author Azadeh Moaveni writes in a new book. 'But while Hillary and Laura were hard at work, Jill Biden appeared to have gone missing.'

The call is detailed in The East Wing: Power, Intrigue, and the Untold Story of America's First Ladies, in which Moaveni traces Jill's time in the position from its promising start to her alleged Lady Macbeth-esque role trying to keep her ailing husband in power when he was up for re-election.

Less than a year before the Kabul incident, the omens had been good when Jill's husband won the 2020 election, inheriting a country with a population that was bruised, exhausted and economically depressed after the Covid-19 pandemic and a tumultuous Trump presidency.

Schools and families were struggling to get back to normal, but 'Jill was one of the few messengers in the administration who resonated with mothers and teachers, who was a teacher herself,' Moaveni writes. She was also politically seasoned, having been at the side of her husband during his career as a senator then serving as Second Lady when he was Vice President to Barack Obama.

But there were early signs that her allegiances were not primarily to the American people, Moaveni claims, but to a husband she had married when she was 26 years old, and to a family which had gone through intense personal turmoil and tragedy. 

During Joe Biden's campaign for the presidency, Jill had visited the squalid Matamoros migrant encampment in Mexico just over the US border and penned an emotional op-ed in the Wall Street Journal asking, 'is this what we have become?' in Trump's America.

But within months of Biden assuming office, with migration on the southern border proving unpopular with voters, she quietly abandoned her initiative to reunite migrant families, a pattern she would repeat throughout her husband's presidency, The East Wing claims.

'Most First Ladies were like this to a degree. But Jill was singular in the way she subsumed herself into Joe's presidency,' writes Moaveni.

'She supported only causes that made him look good and abandoned them the moment they didn't. Any subject that proved awkward to the Biden administration she would generally avoid, even when it related directly to her brand as an educator and an advocate for women.'

Case in point, at the time of the aforementioned fall of Kabul, Jill was involved in an initiative called Joining Forces which supported military families, but in their hour of need, her team had other priorities, the book claims, which was to stop 'all activities that might expose the First Lady to public anger.'

'They had a huge fear of doing anything at bases, they were just petrified,' a former staffer told Moaveni. 'Even though this was when military communities needed support.'

Jill put out a statement mourning the loss of lives a day after a suicide bomb at Kabul airport killed 13 US Service members and more than 170 Afghan civilians, telling military families: 'My heart is with you as you navigate what comes next.'

She avoided any mention of the political ramifications of the withdrawal at the time, although she acknowledged in her recent biography, View From The East Wing, that the fall of Kabul was a 'turning point for Joe's administration.'

Jill's unerring loyalty can be traced back, Moaveni writes, to the start. When she married Joe in 1977, she inherited a family marked by tragedy. Biden's wife Neilia and their 13-month-old daughter Naomi were killed in a car accident five years earlier.

Their sons Hunter and Beau survived, and Jill had the difficult task of becoming 'both stepmother and substitute mother, tending to their lives as Joe commuted to Washington to build his political career.' 

In 1981, Jill and Joe's daughter, Ashley, was born, but personal upheaval and tragedy followed the three children into adulthood. Beau died of brain cancer in 2015. Both Hunter and Ashley struggled with addiction, with Hunter's very public meltdowns triggering a string of crises for the Bidens.

The book details how Joe and Jill initially refused to publicly acknowledge the existence of a little granddaughter called Navy Roberts, whom Hunter Biden had fathered between his marriages. It took a scathing New York Times article in 2023 for them to relent and speak about her.

The article by Maureen Dowd said the Bidens' reluctance to publicly embrace the child 'reveals is how dated and inauthentic the 80-year-old president's view of family is.'

A few weeks later, Joe Biden put out a statement saying he and Jill wanted the best for all their grandchildren, 'including Navy,' but it was 'not a political issue, it's a family matter.' Jill's recent biography is dedicated to her daughter and her granddaughters, but Navy is not listed among them.

The controversy highlighted how tangled their family life had become.

'Both Bidens were carrying out their roles while parenting adult children on the brink – of relapse into addiction, of legal and financial ruin,' writes Moaveni.

This desire to protect the family's privacy led to a number of political decisions, including the appointment of Anthony Bernal as Jill's senior advisor, a powerful gatekeeper variously described as Jill's 'work husband,' and the Biden 'marriage counsellor.'

His overriding attribute? Fierce loyalty to the Biden clan, and to Jill in particular.

'He never stopped wanting to hold her purse,' one insider told Moaveni. 'I think he would crawl into the coffin with her.'

The book goes on: 'Jill's approach to being First Lady was to act as Joe's lead messenger, and this suited Bernal. Her activities never took him out of his comfort zone. Instead, Bernal excelled as the guardian of the Bidens' privacy, and this made him indispensable and the sole staffer in the East Wing to hold real power.'

But by keeping a tight cabal of long-time loyalists and 'Biden people' around her rather than innovative thinkers, Jill was left with 'an aura of blandness,' the book observes: 'They were all respected hands but not the sort of brilliant policy minds, politicos and PR A-listers that Michelle Obama had brought in.' 

The result was an uninspiring tenure as First Lady in which projects including the migration initiative and funding for community colleges were championed then quietly dropped. 

Her initiative to provide free community college education failed when it was dropped from a broader spending bill, and while Jill said at the time that she was 'disappointed,' one insider told Moaveni: 'I didn't get the sense that she was on fire about it.'

'Over the course of four years, her First Ladyship unfolded as exceedingly narrow, even conservative,' Moaveni writes.

'She never pursued a distinct project through which the public could get a sense of her – of her personality, what she cared about and the texture of her beliefs and commitments. She stood steadfastly by her man and squeezed herself into such a narrow, Joe-centric persona that public opinion about the two of them essentially merged.'

But then came Joe Biden's declining health as he was running for a second term, and a chance for Jill to step in and prevent a looming electoral disaster for the Democratic Party.

In March 2024, some former White House staff started to raise the alarm, and the concerns mounted heading into the now infamous June 27, 2024, debate with Donald Trump.

The East Wing details how Jill was consumed in early June by Hunter's firearms trial and multiple official functions. At the same time, Joe developed a cold and appeared 'almost catatonic' to some big donors. He failed to recognize George Clooney, an incident about which the actor penned a scathing op-ed.

After Biden's stumbling and shambolic debate performance laid bare his age-related shortcomings, many questioned if Jill should have stepped in.

'Many senior Democrats blamed her, along with the rest of the family and his close aides, for hiding his condition,' Moaveni writes.

'Surely she had known how diminished he was, and if she knew, why had she not persuaded him to step down… as First Lady, she was the most intimate, public face of the campaign persuading Americans that he was fit to serve another term.'

Jill hailed her husband's debate performance and said he did 'such a great job.' But while she was publicly congratulating him, she admits in her recent biography that privately she was deeply concerned about her husband, and was worried he was having a stroke during the debate. 

She writes: 'It felt like we were watching an AI hologram of the man we knew, and the hologram was glitching.'

But at the time, even as the debate was attracting scathing feedback, she put on a brave face, appearing on the cover of Vogue four days later, wearing a Ralph Lauren tuxedo dress under the headline: 'We Will Decide Our Future.'

'The headline alluded to the rollback around women's rights, but landing four days after the debate, it appeared to convey that Jill was the key figure, along with Joe himself, in deciding the country's future,' the book observes.

While the magazine article had been planned months in advance, the decision to go ahead with it despite the awkward timing fueled the narrative of Jill as a 'Lady Macbeth' figure, so seduced by her proximity to power that she hid his age-related decline.

Even her political allies have dropped the reference, with Alexandra Pelosi, the daughter of former Democratic House speaker Nancy Pelosi, referring to her as Lady McBiden in 2025.

Jill has said during an appearance on The View last year that such comments were 'very hurtful' and said she did not have her husband 'sequestered in some place' to hide any cognitive decline.

The Daily Mail has reached out to Joe and Jill Biden for comment.

Joe Biden eventually stepped down as the Democratic candidate to make way for Kamala Harris at the end of July 2024, leading to Trump's resounding success at the election later that year and leaving Jill Biden with little legacy to speak of.

In her biography, Jill concedes that not adequately addressing concerns about Biden's health led to more questions, but she defends her time as First Lady and addresses the delicate tightrope she had to walk.

'Being First Lady could feel like a catch-22,' she writes. 'You were encouraged to use your platform to do good, but not to be too aggressive in pursuing policy goals, lest you be seen as overreaching. If you knew too little about what you were talking about, then you were an embarrassment. If you knew too much, you were trying to rule the world.
news.summary: There were early signs that her allegiances were not primarily to the American people, but to a husband and to a family which had gone through intense personal turmoil and tragedy.

news.title: Comment on Vance, Rubio, Ossoff and Buttigieg lead 2028 White House hopefuls by The Weekly Dispatch · Week to Sunday, 15 November 2026
news.text:
Four potential contenders in the 2028 race for the White House have caught American voters’ attention with their early jockeying: Republicans JD Vance and Marco Rubio and Democrats Jon Ossoff and Pete ​Buttigieg, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll.

None of the four has yet formally launched a campaign and the parties’ 2028 nominating contests are more than a year away, leaving plenty of time ‌for new contenders to emerge and for voters’ views to change.

The Misinformation Monitor newsletter rounds up international misinformation narratives, with a “Real or Fake?” quiz in every edition. Sign up here.

Some 45% of Republican voters polled said they believed Secretary of State Rubio would be an “excellent” presidential candidate, with 43% saying the same of Vice President Vance. Former Transportation Secretary Buttigieg and US Senator Ossoff, of Georgia, each got that rating from 29% of Democratic voters.

The poll, which surveyed 1,705 US adults nationwide including roughly 500 registered voters from each party and was completed on Monday, had a margin of error of 5 percentage points for Republican and Democratic ​voters.

President Donald Trump, struggling with an approval rating near the lowest of his career, looms large over the conversation for both parties. Republicans are divided on whether they want a candidate who breaks with Trump ​or follows in his footsteps, while Democrats, who are flying high after routing Republicans in the November 3 congressional elections, are divided on how aggressively to go after ⁠the president, such as through impeachment.

Trump has quizzed allies on whom they prefer Vance or Rubio and in a Sunday interview with CBS’s “60 Minutes” said he would “not necessarily” make an endorsement in the Republican primary.

‘MANAGED TO DO HIS ​JOB’

Barbara Rezner, an attorney in Florida who voted for Trump in the last three presidential elections, said she prefers Rubio over Vance, whom she considers too far to the right and too close to the president.

“Rubio has managed ​to do his job. He’s stayed off most people’s radar because he hasn’t done anything too far left, too far right, too crazy,” Rezner said.

The modest but growing dissatisfaction with Trump among Republicans is centered on the president’s decision to launch a war on Iran that has driven fuel prices higher. Rubio has been notably absent from many of the so-far fruitless peace talks with Iran despite being the nation’s top diplomat. Vance has shown signs of wanting to distance himself as well, saying publicly that the Republican drubbing ​in the midterm elections owed to the war with Iran.

A dozen-odd other Republicans are also in the national conversation over 2028 contenders, with Florida Governor Ron DeSantis among the best regarded, with 32% of Republicans rating him ​as an excellent option. Others – like Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr., and Texas US Senator Ted Cruz – have their fans, but also many detractors.

Item 1 of 4 U.S. Vice President JD Vance President and Secretary of State Marco Rubio attend U.S. President Donald Trump’s address to the nation about election security, at the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., July 16, 2026. SAUL LOEB/Pool via REUTERS/File Photo

[1/4]U.S. Vice President JD Vance President and Secretary of State Marco Rubio attend U.S. President Donald Trump’s address to the nation about election security, at the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., July 16, 2026. SAUL LOEB/Pool via REUTERS/File Photo Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab

OSSOFF AND BUTTIGIEG

Among Democrats, Ossoff is at the top of many voters’ lists, with 29% of the party’s registered ‌voters rating ⁠him as excellent. Ossoff has grabbed headlines in recent months by calling Trump corrupt and unfit for office in unusually direct language, and last week he won his re-election race by 18 percentage points in Georgia, a state Trump carried by 2 points in 2024.

Buttigieg also gets the excellent rating from 29% of Democrats. Buttigieg also ran for president in 2020 and is better known nationally than Ossoff.

About one in five Democrats say they have never heard of Buttigieg, compared to roughly one in three who say the same about Ossoff. Very few Republicans are unfamiliar with Vance, but about one in six said they do not know who Rubio is. For candidates in either party, starting ​the election cycle with more name recognition can save ​money that would be spent getting the candidate’s ⁠name out, but examples abound of little-known candidates catching fire during the campaign, as happened with former President Bill Clinton.

Buttigieg and Ossoff are considered moderates among Democrats, and that appeals to Democratic voters like Ed Blair, a retired pig farmer in southern Illinois, who gives Buttigieg a better rating in part because Ossoff is less familiar.

“I do favor ​the more moderate candidates over the more progressive ones,” said Blair, who is wary of proposed major shifts like expanding federal Medicare health insurance coverage from ​all seniors to everyone in the ⁠country. Blair would prefer gradual shifts, such as expanding Medicare to cover all children. “In going towards some of the progressive policies, small steps need to be taken rather than large ones to give people time to adapt.”

The Reuters/Ipsos poll shows other well-known moderates – like former Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump in the 2024 presidential election, and California Governor Gavin Newsom – each get “excellent candidate” ratings of 23%, higher than the 15% of Democrats who view progressive stalwart Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, ⁠a US representative ​for New York, that way.

Ocasio-Cortez told CNN after the midterms that impeaching Trump should be an option on the table, while Buttigieg told the New ​Yorker magazine he is “not very interested” in impeachment.

Elaine Kamarck, a Democratic strategist, cautioned against reading too deeply into the public’s current views this far out from the 2028 election. “It’s a world away,” Kamarck said. “There are lots of people in both parties who are still deciding if they ​are going to run. You might be able to predict who will run, but you certainly don’t know anything about who is going to be ahead.”

Via Reuters
